stem: According to the Nagpur Road Plan classification, roads are grouped into:
options: National highways, state highways, district roads and village roads
explanation: District roads are further split into major and other district roads.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 1

stem: National Highways in India are the responsibility of:
explanation: NHAI executes most national highway projects.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 1

stem: A state highway is defined as a road that:
options: Connects district headquarters and important cities within a state to national highways
explanation: It acts as the arterial route of the state road network.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 1

stem: Major district roads are those that:
options: Connect areas of production with markets and link with state highways
explanation: Other district roads serve rural areas of production.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 1

stem: Village roads or rural roads primarily:
options: Connect villages to each other and to the nearest higher category road
explanation: PMGSY targets all weather connectivity to villages.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 1

stem: An expressway is characterised by:
options: Full access control, divided carriageway and grade separated intersections
explanation: High design speed and safety are its main objectives.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 1

stem: Classification of roads based on traffic volume divides them into:
options: Heavy, medium and light traffic roads
explanation: Classification by load gives class I to class V roads.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 1

stem: Based on the type of carriageway surface, roads are classified as:
explanation: Surfaced and unsurfaced is an equivalent classification.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 1

topic: Road development in India and current road projects
stem: The Jayakar Committee of 1927 recommended:
options: Levy of a petrol tax to create a central road fund and a semi-official technical body
explanation: This led to formation of the Indian Roads Congress in 1934.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 1

topic: Road development in India and current road projects
stem: The Indian Roads Congress was established in:
explanation: It frames standards and specifications for Indian roads.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 1

topic: Road development in India and current road projects
stem: The Nagpur Road Plan covered the twenty year period:
explanation: It was the first attempt at systematic road development planning.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 1

topic: Road development in India and current road projects
stem: The star and grid pattern of road network was proposed in the:
explanation: The road length was computed from the area and number of towns.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 1

topic: Road development in India and current road projects
stem: The Bombay Road Plan covering 1961 to 1981 aimed at a road density of:
options: 32 kilometres per 100 square kilometres of area
explanation: The Nagpur plan target had been 16 km per 100 sq km.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 1

topic: Road development in India and current road projects
stem: The Lucknow Road Plan is also known as the:
options: Third twenty year road development plan for 1981 to 2001
explanation: It introduced the concept of expressways in India.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 1

topic: Road development in India and current road projects
stem: The Golden Quadrilateral project connects:
explanation: It forms part of the National Highways Development Project.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 1

topic: Road development in India and current road projects
stem: Pradhan Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana aims to provide:
options: All weather road connectivity to unconnected habitations
explanation: It was launched in the year 2000.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 1

topic: Road development in India and current road projects
stem: The Bharatmala Pariyojana focuses on:
options: Economic corridors, border roads and coastal connectivity
explanation: It aims to optimise the efficiency of freight movement.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 1

topic: Road development in India and current road projects
stem: The North South and East West corridors of NHDP connect:
options: Srinagar to Kanyakumari and Silchar to Porbandar
explanation: They form Phase II of the National Highways Development Project.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 1

stem: Highway alignment refers to:
options: The position or layout of the centre line of the highway on the ground
explanation: It has both horizontal and vertical components.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 1

stem: The basic requirements of an ideal highway alignment are:
explanation: These four requirements often conflict and need compromise.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 1

stem: An obligatory point through which the alignment must pass could be:
options: An intermediate town, a bridge site or a mountain pass
A religious place to be avoided
explanation: Obligatory points to avoid include marshy land and costly structures.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 1

stem: The engineering surveys for a new highway are conducted in the sequence:
options: Map study, reconnaissance, preliminary survey and final location survey
explanation: Each stage progressively narrows the corridor of study.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 1

stem: Map study of a proposed alignment is done using:
options: Topographic maps such as Survey of India sheets
explanation: It gives possible alternative routes at the desk stage.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 1

stem: Reconnaissance survey involves:
options: A rapid field inspection of alternative routes identified in the map study
explanation: Simple instruments such as an Abney level are used.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 1

stem: The preliminary survey of a highway is carried out to:
options: Compare alternative alignments and estimate quantities and cost
Set out the final centre line
explanation: Detailed topographic and soil surveys are made along each route.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 1

stem: The final location and detailed survey establishes:
options: The centre line on the ground with pegs and detailed level data
explanation: Data from it forms the basis of the detailed project report.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 1

stem: In hilly terrain, ruling gradient is a controlling factor of alignment because:
options: Excessive gradients increase operating cost and reduce safety
explanation: Compensation in gradient is applied at sharp curves.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 1

stem: A detailed project report for a highway typically includes:
options: Survey data, design details, drawings, quantities, cost estimate and environmental clearance
explanation: It forms the basis for tendering and construction.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 1

stem: Deviation of an alignment to avoid a costly land acquisition is justified only when:
options: The increase in road length and cost is less than the saving achieved
explanation: An economic comparison of alternatives decides the issue.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 1

stem: Urban roads are classified by the Indian Roads Congress into:
options: Arterial, sub-arterial, collector and local streets
explanation: Access control decreases from arterial to local streets.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 1

topic: Road development in India and current road projects
stem: The Nagpur Road Plan was the first twenty year road development plan in India.
explanation: It covered the period 1943 to 1961 and introduced the star and grid pattern.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 1

stem: The final location survey precedes the reconnaissance survey.
explanation: Reconnaissance comes early; final location survey is the last stage.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 1

stem:
Assertion (A): Highway alignment is fixed after several stages of survey.
Reason (R): Each successive survey stage provides more accurate data over a narrower corridor.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: This avoids the cost of detailed survey over all alternative routes.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 1

stem:
Assertion (A): National highways are maintained by the central government.
Reason (R): They form the main arterial network connecting states, ports and capitals.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Their national importance justifies central responsibility and funding.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 1

stem: Which are basic requirements of an ideal highway alignment?
options: Easy for construction and traffic operation
explanation: Curves should be minimised, not maximised; economy is the fourth requirement.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 1

stem: The standard width of a single lane carriageway for rural highways as per IRC is:
explanation: Two lane roads without kerbs are 7.0 m wide.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 2

stem: Camber is provided on a road surface mainly to:
options: Drain rain water quickly to the sides
explanation: It is the transverse slope of the carriageway.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 2

stem: The recommended camber for a bituminous surfaced road in a heavy rainfall area is about:
explanation: Cement concrete roads need flatter camber than earth roads.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 2

stem: Right of way is defined as:
options: The total land width acquired for the road along its alignment
explanation: It provides for future widening and utilities.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 2

stem: The main function of a shoulder is to:
options: Provide lateral support to the pavement and space for stopped vehicles
explanation: Shoulders should be rougher than the carriageway to discourage use.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 2

stem: A median or traffic separator is provided to:
options: Separate opposing streams of traffic and reduce head on collisions
explanation: It also shields headlight glare from opposing vehicles.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 2

stem: Kerbs on an urban road are provided to:
options: Indicate the boundary between the carriageway and the footpath or shoulder
explanation: Barrier type kerbs are 150 to 200 mm high.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 2

stem: Road margin includes:
options: Shoulders, parking lanes, footpaths, cycle tracks and frontage roads
explanation: These are portions of the right of way outside the carriageway.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 2

stem: Width of a two lane carriageway with raised kerbs is:
explanation: Extra width is provided for the effect of the kerbs.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 2

stem: Stopping sight distance is the sum of:
options: Lag distance during reaction time and braking distance
explanation: IRC adopts a total reaction time of 2.5 seconds.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 2

stem: The braking distance for a vehicle of speed v on a level road with longitudinal friction f is:
explanation: On a gradient, f is replaced by f plus or minus the grade.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 2

stem: The perception and brake reaction time adopted by IRC for stopping sight distance is:
explanation: It covers perception, intellection, emotion and volition.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 2

stem: Overtaking sight distance depends on:
options: Speeds of the overtaking, overtaken and opposing vehicles and acceleration
explanation: It equals d1 plus d2 plus d3 on two way two lane roads.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 2

stem: On a divided highway with one way traffic, overtaking sight distance required is:
explanation: There is no opposing vehicle component d3.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 2

stem: The height of the driver's eye assumed for sight distance calculations by IRC is:
explanation: The object height is taken as 0.15 m.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 2

stem: Intermediate sight distance is generally taken as:
explanation: It is provided where overtaking sight distance cannot be achieved.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 2

stem: On a descending gradient, the stopping sight distance:
options: Increases because the effective friction is reduced
explanation: The gradient term is subtracted from the friction coefficient.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 2

stem: Superelevation is provided on a horizontal curve to:
options: Counteract the centrifugal force acting on a vehicle
explanation: The outer edge is raised with respect to the inner edge.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 2

stem: The maximum superelevation allowed on plain and rolling terrain roads by IRC is:
explanation: For hilly terrain without snow, 10 percent is allowed.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 2

stem: The equilibrium superelevation for speed v, radius R is given by:
explanation: With friction, e plus f equals v squared over gR.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 2

stem: The design coefficient of lateral friction adopted by IRC is:
explanation: Longitudinal friction is taken as 0.35 to 0.40.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 2

stem: A transition curve is introduced between a straight and a circular curve to:
options: Gradually introduce centrifugal force and superelevation
explanation: A spiral or clothoid is recommended by IRC.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 2

stem: Extra widening on a horizontal curve consists of:
explanation: Mechanical widening accounts for the off tracking of rear wheels.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 2

stem: The length of transition curve by the rate of change of centrifugal acceleration criterion is:
explanation: C usually ranges from 0.5 to 0.8 metre per second cubed.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 2

stem: Set back distance on a horizontal curve is required to:
options: Clear obstructions on the inner side so that sight distance is available
explanation: It depends on the curve radius, sight distance and road width.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 2

topic: Design of vertical alignment and intersections
stem: Ruling gradient is also known as:
explanation: Limiting and exceptional gradients are steeper and used sparingly.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 2

topic: Design of vertical alignment and intersections
stem: Grade compensation at a horizontal curve is applied because:
options: Curve resistance is added to the gradient resistance
explanation: IRC gives compensation as 30 plus R over R percent, limited to 75 over R.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 2

topic: Design of vertical alignment and intersections
stem: A summit curve is designed on the basis of:
explanation: Valley curves are designed for comfort and headlight sight distance.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 2

topic: Design of vertical alignment and intersections
stem: The shape of a summit curve generally recommended is:
explanation: A parabola gives a constant rate of change of grade.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 2

topic: Design of vertical alignment and intersections
stem: A rotary intersection is most suitable when:
options: Traffic volumes are moderate and the number of intersecting roads is four to seven
Only two roads meet at right angles
explanation: Rotaries convert crossing conflicts into weaving manoeuvres.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 2

topic: Design of vertical alignment and intersections
stem: A channelised intersection improves safety by:
options: Increasing the number of conflict points
Using islands and markings to guide traffic into definite paths
explanation: It reduces the area of conflict at an at-grade intersection.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 2

stem: Overtaking sight distance is always greater than stopping sight distance.
explanation: Overtaking requires a much longer clear distance than merely stopping.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 2

stem: Superelevation is limited so that slow moving vehicles do not slide inward.
explanation: IRC therefore caps superelevation at 7 percent in plain terrain.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 2

stem:
Assertion (A): A transition curve is provided at both ends of a circular curve.
Reason (R): It allows superelevation and extra widening to be introduced gradually.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Sudden introduction of centrifugal force would be unsafe and uncomfortable.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 2

topic: Design of vertical alignment and intersections
stem:
Assertion (A): Valley curves are designed for night time headlight sight distance.
Reason (R): At night the available sight distance on a valley curve is limited by headlight beam spread.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Daytime visibility on valley curves is unobstructed.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 2

stem: Which of the following are cross sectional elements of a highway?
explanation: Sight distance is a geometric design control, not a cross section element.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 2

stem: The three main components studied in traffic characteristics are:
explanation: Their interaction governs traffic behaviour and safety.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 3

stem: The PIEV time in driver characteristics stands for:
explanation: It represents the total reaction time of a driver.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 3

stem: The design vehicle governing the geometric design of intersections is:
options: The largest vehicle expected to use the facility regularly
explanation: Its turning radius determines the intersection geometry.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 3

stem: Vehicular characteristics affecting road design include:
options: Dimensions, weight, power and braking capability
explanation: Maximum axle load governs pavement design.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 3

stem: The maximum permissible width of a vehicle in India for road design purposes is about:
explanation: Lane width of 3.75 m accommodates this plus clearance.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 3

stem: Passenger car unit is used to:
options: Convert a mixed traffic stream into an equivalent homogeneous stream
explanation: A car is assigned a PCU value of one.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 3

stem: A traffic volume study measures:
options: The number of vehicles crossing a section in unit time
explanation: It is normally expressed in vehicles or PCU per hour.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 3

stem: Annual average daily traffic is obtained by:
options: Dividing the total yearly traffic volume by 365
explanation: AADT is the basic input for pavement and capacity design.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 3

stem: Spot speed studies are used mainly to:
options: Establish speed limits, sight distance and geometric design values
explanation: The 85th percentile speed is commonly used for speed limits.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 3

stem: The 85th percentile speed represents the speed:
options: Below which 85 percent of vehicles travel
explanation: It is adopted as the safe speed limit for the road.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 3

stem: The 98th percentile speed is used for:
options: Geometric design of highways such as sight distance
explanation: It represents the design speed to be catered for safely.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 3

stem: A speed and delay study by the moving observer method gives:
options: Journey speed, running speed and the causes and magnitude of delay
explanation: It helps identify congested sections and bottlenecks.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 3

stem: Origin and destination studies are carried out to:
options: Plan new road links, bypasses and terminal facilities
explanation: Methods include road side interviews and licence plate surveys.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 3

stem: A traffic accident study uses the collision diagram to:
options: Show the type and pattern of accidents at a location
explanation: A condition diagram shows the physical features of the site.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 3

stem: The accident rate per million vehicle kilometres is calculated as:
options: Number of accidents divided by road length
Number of accidents times one million divided by total vehicle kilometres
explanation: It permits comparison between roads with different traffic volumes.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 3

stem: The peak hour factor for a road is defined as:
options: Peak hour volume divided by four times the peak fifteen minute volume
explanation: It measures the uniformity of flow within the peak hour.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 3

stem: The fundamental relation of traffic flow is:
options: Flow equals density divided by speed
Flow equals density times space mean speed
explanation: It is written as q equals k times v.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 3

stem: Traffic density is defined as:
options: The number of vehicles occupying a unit length of road at an instant
explanation: It is usually expressed in vehicles per kilometre.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 3

stem: Space mean speed is:
options: The harmonic mean of the spot speeds of vehicles on a stretch
The arithmetic mean of spot speeds
explanation: Time mean speed is the arithmetic mean and is always greater.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 3

stem: According to Greenshields, the speed density relationship is:
explanation: This gives a parabolic flow density curve.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 3

stem: Capacity of a road is the:
options: Maximum hourly rate at which vehicles can reasonably traverse a section
explanation: Practical capacity or design service volume is lower than the theoretical.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 3

stem: Level of service is a qualitative measure describing:
options: Operating conditions in a traffic stream as perceived by drivers
explanation: It is graded from A, free flow, to F, forced flow.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 3

stem: Level of service F corresponds to:
options: Forced or breakdown flow with stop and go conditions
explanation: Demand exceeds capacity and queues form.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 3

stem: Theoretical maximum capacity of a single lane with average spacing S metres and speed V kmph is:
options: 1000 V divided by S vehicles per hour
explanation: The spacing is derived from the space headway of vehicles.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 3

stem: Jam density occurs when:
options: Vehicles are bumper to bumper and speed and flow are zero
explanation: It is the maximum possible density on the road.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 3

stem: Maximum flow on the Greenshields parabolic curve occurs at:
options: Half the free flow speed and half the jam density
explanation: Maximum flow equals one quarter of the product of free speed and jam density.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 3

stem: Time headway is defined as:
options: The time interval between passages of successive vehicles at a section
explanation: Its reciprocal multiplied by 3600 gives flow per hour.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 3

stem: Parking studies determine:
options: Parking demand, accumulation, duration and turnover
explanation: Parking index measures the utilisation of available space.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 3

stem: An automatic traffic counter using a pneumatic tube records:
options: Axle impulses which are converted to vehicle counts
explanation: Two axle vehicles produce two impulses per passage.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 3

stem: Traffic engineering is defined as the branch dealing with:
options: Planning, geometric design and traffic operations of roads for safe and efficient movement
explanation: It also covers relationships with other modes of transport.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 3

stem: Time mean speed is always greater than or equal to space mean speed.
explanation: The difference equals the variance of speeds divided by the space mean speed.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 3

stem: The 85th percentile speed is used to fix the upper speed limit on a road.
explanation: It is regarded as the safe speed that most drivers do not exceed.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 3

stem:
Assertion (A): Level of service deteriorates as the volume to capacity ratio increases.
Reason (R): Higher volume to capacity ratios reduce manoeuvring freedom and speed.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: At a ratio approaching unity, flow becomes unstable.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 3

stem:
Assertion (A): Origin and destination surveys are essential before planning a bypass.
Reason (R): They reveal how much traffic merely passes through the town without stopping.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Only through traffic benefits from a bypass.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 3

stem: Which of the following are recognised traffic engineering studies?
explanation: The CBR test is a soil strength test for pavement design.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 3

unit_title: Traffic regulation and control Traffic regulation and control Design of
stem: Traffic signs are broadly classified into:
explanation: Regulatory signs are mandatory and enforceable by law.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 4

unit_title: Traffic regulation and control Traffic regulation and control Design of
stem: Warning signs in India are generally:
options: Equilateral triangles with the apex upwards and a red border
explanation: They caution drivers about hazards ahead.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 4

unit_title: Traffic regulation and control Traffic regulation and control Design of
stem: The STOP sign is:
options: Octagonal in shape with white lettering on red
explanation: Its unique shape allows recognition even from behind.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 4

unit_title: Traffic regulation and control Traffic regulation and control Design of
stem: A continuous centre line marking on a road indicates:
options: Crossing or overtaking across the line is prohibited
explanation: A broken line permits crossing with care.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 4

unit_title: Traffic regulation and control Traffic regulation and control Design of
stem: The main objective of traffic signal control is to:
options: Assign right of way to conflicting streams in time so as to reduce conflicts
explanation: Signals separate conflicting movements in time rather than space.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 4

unit_title: Traffic regulation and control Traffic regulation and control Design of
stem: Webster's method is used to determine:
options: Optimum signal cycle length giving minimum delay
explanation: The optimum cycle is (1.5L+5) divided by (1 minus Y).
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 4

unit_title: Traffic regulation and control Traffic regulation and control Design of
stem: In Webster's formula, the term L represents:
explanation: Y is the sum of the critical flow ratios of all phases.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 4

unit_title: Traffic regulation and control Traffic regulation and control Design of
stem: A fixed time signal:
options: Operates on a preset cycle regardless of actual traffic demand
explanation: Vehicle actuated signals adjust green time to demand.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 4

unit_title: Traffic regulation and control Traffic regulation and control Design of
stem: A linked or coordinated signal system provides:
options: A green wave allowing platoons to pass successive signals without stopping
explanation: Offsets between signals are set from the platoon travel time.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 4

unit_title: Traffic regulation and control Traffic regulation and control Design of
stem: Traffic islands used for pedestrian refuge are classified as:
explanation: Divisional islands separate opposing flows on undivided roads.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 4

unit_title: Traffic regulation and control Traffic regulation and control Design of
stem: An intersection where roads meet at the same level is called:
explanation: Grade separation uses different levels for the crossing roads.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 4

unit_title: Traffic regulation and control Traffic regulation and control Design of
stem: The number of conflict points at an uncontrolled four leg intersection is:
explanation: These comprise 16 crossing, 4 merging and 4 diverging points.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 4

unit_title: Traffic regulation and control Traffic regulation and control Design of
stem: A rotary intersection converts crossing conflicts into:
explanation: All traffic moves in one direction around the central island.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 4

unit_title: Traffic regulation and control Traffic regulation and control Design of
stem: The recommended weaving angle for a rotary is:
explanation: Small weaving angles allow smooth merging and diverging.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 4

unit_title: Traffic regulation and control Traffic regulation and control Design of
stem: The design speed usually adopted for rotaries in rural areas is:
explanation: For urban rotaries 30 kmph is generally adopted.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 4

unit_title: Traffic regulation and control Traffic regulation and control Design of
stem: The weaving length of a rotary should preferably be at least:
explanation: Adequate length allows safe merging and diverging.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 4

unit_title: Traffic regulation and control Traffic regulation and control Design of
stem: A trumpet interchange is generally used at:
options: A T junction of a major and a minor highway
explanation: A cloverleaf is used at four leg grade separated crossings.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 4

unit_title: Traffic regulation and control Traffic regulation and control Design of
stem: A diamond interchange requires:
options: Less land and is suitable where the minor road can be signalised
explanation: It has four ramps meeting the minor road at grade.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 4

unit_title: Traffic regulation and control Traffic regulation and control Design of
stem: Channelisation at an intersection is achieved by:
options: Islands, pavement markings and auxiliary lanes that define vehicle paths
explanation: It reduces the conflict area and controls turning speeds.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 4

unit_title: Traffic regulation and control Traffic regulation and control Design of
stem: Grade separated intersections are justified when:
options: Traffic volumes are very high and at-grade capacity is exceeded
Land is scarce and cheap traffic
explanation: They eliminate crossing conflicts entirely.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 4

unit_title: Traffic regulation and control Traffic regulation and control Design of
topic: Design of parking facilities and highway lighting
stem: On street parking with vehicles at 90 degrees to the kerb:
options: Accommodates the maximum number of vehicles per unit kerb length
explanation: It also demands the greatest carriageway width for manoeuvring.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 4

unit_title: Traffic regulation and control Traffic regulation and control Design of
topic: Design of parking facilities and highway lighting
stem: Parallel parking is preferred where:
options: The street width is restricted and interference with traffic must be minimum
explanation: It occupies the least carriageway width.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 4

unit_title: Traffic regulation and control Traffic regulation and control Design of
topic: Design of parking facilities and highway lighting
stem: Parking accumulation is defined as:
options: The number of vehicles parked in an area at a specified instant
explanation: Its plot against time gives the parking accumulation curve.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 4

unit_title: Traffic regulation and control Traffic regulation and control Design of
topic: Design of parking facilities and highway lighting
stem: Parking index or occupancy is:
options: The percentage of available parking spaces actually occupied
The number of vehicles per hour
explanation: An index above 90 percent indicates saturation.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 4

unit_title: Traffic regulation and control Traffic regulation and control Design of
topic: Design of parking facilities and highway lighting
stem: Parking turnover indicates:
options: The rate of use of parking spaces, given by vehicles parked per space per time
explanation: High turnover means short duration parking.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 4

unit_title: Traffic regulation and control Traffic regulation and control Design of
topic: Design of parking facilities and highway lighting
stem: Off street parking facilities include:
options: Surface car parks and multi storey parking garages
explanation: They remove parked vehicles from the carriageway entirely.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 4

unit_title: Traffic regulation and control Traffic regulation and control Design of
topic: Design of parking facilities and highway lighting
stem: The main purpose of highway lighting is to:
options: Improve visibility at night and reduce night accidents
explanation: Uniform luminance without glare is the design goal.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 4

unit_title: Traffic regulation and control Traffic regulation and control Design of
topic: Design of parking facilities and highway lighting
stem: In street lighting design, the term lux denotes:
options: Illumination or luminous flux per unit area
explanation: One lux equals one lumen per square metre.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 4

unit_title: Traffic regulation and control Traffic regulation and control Design of
topic: Design of parking facilities and highway lighting
stem: Staggered arrangement of street light poles is generally adopted when:
options: The road width is between one and one and a half times the mounting height
The road is one way only
explanation: Opposite arrangement suits very wide roads.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 4

unit_title: Traffic regulation and control Traffic regulation and control Design of
stem: Speed control devices such as rumble strips are used to:
options: Alert drivers and reduce speed at hazardous locations
explanation: They create noise and vibration warning the driver.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 4

unit_title: Traffic regulation and control Traffic regulation and control Design of
stem: A rotary intersection is suitable for very high traffic volumes exceeding 5000 vehicles per hour.
explanation: Rotaries become inefficient beyond about 3000 vehicles per hour; grade separation is then needed.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 4

unit_title: Traffic regulation and control Traffic regulation and control Design of
topic: Design of parking facilities and highway lighting
stem: Ninety degree parking accommodates more vehicles per unit kerb length than parallel parking.
explanation: But it needs a greater road width for manoeuvring.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 4

unit_title: Traffic regulation and control Traffic regulation and control Design of
stem:
Assertion (A): Signal cycle time should neither be too short nor too long.
Reason (R): Short cycles waste time in frequent lost time and long cycles cause excessive delay.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Webster's optimum cycle balances these two effects.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 4

unit_title: Traffic regulation and control Traffic regulation and control Design of
stem:
Assertion (A): Channelisation reduces accidents at intersections.
Reason (R): It confines vehicles to definite paths and reduces the conflict area.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Islands also provide refuge for pedestrians.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 4

unit_title: Traffic regulation and control Traffic regulation and control Design of
stem: Which are classes of traffic signs used in India?
explanation: There is no structural class of traffic sign.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 4

stem: The California bearing ratio test is used to evaluate:
options: The strength of subgrade soil and pavement materials
explanation: CBR is expressed as a percentage of a standard crushed stone value.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 5

stem: The standard load for CBR at 2.5 mm penetration is:
explanation: At 5 mm penetration the standard load is 2055 kg.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 5

stem: In the CBR test the rate of penetration of the plunger is:
explanation: The plunger has an area of 19.635 square centimetres.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 5

stem: The plate bearing test on subgrade determines:
options: The modulus of subgrade reaction k
explanation: k is used in rigid pavement design.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 5

stem: A good subgrade soil should have:
options: Adequate strength, incompressibility, good drainage and low volume change
explanation: Expansive clays make poor subgrades.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 5

stem: Group index of a soil is computed from:
options: Percentage passing 75 micron sieve, liquid limit and plasticity index
explanation: A higher group index indicates a poorer subgrade.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 5

stem: The Los Angeles abrasion test measures the aggregate property of:
explanation: The maximum permitted value for surface courses is about 30 percent.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 5

stem: The aggregate impact value test measures:
options: Toughness or resistance to sudden shock
explanation: For wearing courses the value should not exceed 30 percent.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 5

stem: The aggregate crushing value test indicates:
options: Resistance of aggregate to gradually applied compressive load
explanation: A value below 30 percent is required for surface courses.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 5

stem: Flakiness index of aggregate is the percentage by weight of particles whose:
options: Least dimension is less than three fifths of the mean dimension
Greatest dimension exceeds nine fifths of the mean
explanation: Elongation index uses the greatest dimension criterion.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 5

stem: The soundness test on aggregates assesses:
options: Resistance to weathering by alternate wetting and drying in sulphate solution
explanation: Sodium or magnesium sulphate solutions are used.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 5

stem: The stripping value test on aggregates evaluates:
options: Adhesion between bitumen and aggregate in the presence of water
explanation: Hydrophilic aggregates such as quartzite strip readily.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 5

stem: Water absorption of aggregates used in pavement should generally not exceed:
explanation: High absorption indicates porous and weak aggregate.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 5

stem: The penetration test on bitumen measures:
options: Consistency or hardness of the bitumen
explanation: It is the depth in tenths of a millimetre penetrated in 5 seconds.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 5

stem: The standard conditions for the bitumen penetration test are:
options: 100 g load, 5 seconds and 25 degrees Celsius
explanation: Grades such as 60 or 70 refer to this penetration value.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 5

stem: The ductility test on bitumen determines:
options: The distance in centimetres a briquette elongates before breaking
explanation: A minimum ductility of about 50 cm is generally required.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 5

stem: The ring and ball apparatus is used for determining the:
explanation: It is the temperature at which the bitumen attains a specified softness.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 5

stem: Cutback bitumen is prepared by:
options: Blending bitumen with a volatile solvent to reduce viscosity
explanation: Rapid, medium and slow curing types depend on the solvent used.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 5

stem: Bitumen emulsion consists of:
options: Bitumen dispersed as fine globules in water with an emulsifier
explanation: It permits cold application and is used for maintenance work.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 5

stem: The flash point of bitumen is:
options: The lowest temperature at which vapours momentarily ignite on applying a flame
explanation: It indicates the safe heating temperature during construction.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 5

stem: The Marshall stability test determines:
options: The maximum load a compacted bituminous specimen carries at 60 degrees Celsius
explanation: Flow value is the deformation at maximum load, in units of 0.25 mm.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 5

stem: In the Marshall method, the specimen is compacted with:
options: A 4.5 kg hammer falling 45 cm, applying 75 blows on each face
explanation: The specimen is 101.6 mm in diameter and 63.5 mm high.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 5

stem: Optimum bitumen content by the Marshall method is generally taken as the average of contents corresponding to:
options: Maximum stability, maximum unit weight and 4 percent air voids
explanation: The mix must also satisfy VMA and VFB requirements.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 5

stem: Bituminous concrete differs from bituminous macadam mainly in that it:
options: Uses a dense well graded mix with filler giving an impervious wearing course
explanation: Bituminous macadam is an open graded base or binder course.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 5

stem: The grade of cement concrete generally specified for rigid pavements is at least:
explanation: Pavement quality concrete must resist flexural stresses and abrasion.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 5

stem: The design of rigid pavements is based primarily on:
options: Flexural strength or modulus of rupture of concrete
explanation: Westergaard's analysis uses the flexural stress criterion.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 5

stem: Desirable properties of cement concrete for pavements include:
options: Adequate flexural strength, workability, durability and abrasion resistance
explanation: Low water cement ratio improves most of these properties.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 5

stem: Air entrainment in pavement concrete is beneficial because it:
options: Improves workability and resistance to freeze thaw damage
explanation: Air content of about 4 to 6 percent is typical.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 5

stem: The modulus of rupture of pavement concrete is normally determined by:
options: A flexure test on a beam specimen under third point loading
explanation: It relates approximately to the square root of compressive strength.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 5

stem: Polished stone value of aggregate is important for:
options: Skid resistance of the wearing course
explanation: Aggregates that polish quickly reduce surface friction.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 5

stem: The softening point of bitumen decreases as the grade becomes harder.
explanation: Harder grades have lower penetration but higher softening points.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 5

stem: A higher CBR value permits a thinner pavement for the same traffic.
explanation: Stronger subgrade needs less pavement thickness above it.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 5

stem:
Assertion (A): Flaky and elongated aggregates are undesirable in pavement construction.
Reason (R): They break easily under load and produce poor interlock and workability.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: IRC therefore limits the combined flakiness and elongation index.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 5

stem:
Assertion (A): Bitumen emulsions can be applied without heating.
Reason (R): The bitumen is already dispersed in water so its viscosity at ambient temperature is low.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: They are ideal for pothole repair in wet weather.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 5

stem: Which tests are performed on road aggregates?
explanation: The ring and ball test is performed on bitumen, not aggregate.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 5

stem: A flexible pavement transmits wheel load to the subgrade:
options: Through grain to grain contact with load spread over a wider area with depth
explanation: Rigid pavements distribute load through slab bending action.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 6

stem: The typical component layers of a flexible pavement from top are:
options: Surface course, base course, sub-base and subgrade
explanation: Each layer must be stronger than the one below it.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 6

stem: Boussinesq's theory for flexible pavement analysis assumes the pavement to be:
options: A homogeneous, isotropic, elastic half space
explanation: Burmister's theory extends this to layered systems.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 6

stem: The vertical stress at depth z below a point load P by Boussinesq's equation on the axis is:
explanation: Stress decreases with the square of depth below the load.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 6

stem: The equivalent single wheel load concept is used for:
options: Converting a dual wheel assembly into a single wheel producing the same effect
explanation: ESWL depends on depth, spacing and tyre contact radius.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 6

stem: The vehicle damage factor expresses:
options: Number of standard axles equivalent to one commercial vehicle
explanation: The fourth power law relates axle load to damage.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 6

stem: The standard axle load used in Indian flexible pavement design is:
explanation: Traffic is expressed in million standard axles.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 6

stem: The two critical strains considered in mechanistic flexible pavement design are:
options: Horizontal tensile strain at the bottom of the bituminous layer and vertical compressive strain on the subgrade
Only tensile strain in the subgrade
Only compressive strain in the surface
explanation: They control fatigue cracking and rutting respectively.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 6

stem: Factors affecting the design and performance of flexible pavements include:
options: Traffic loading, subgrade strength, climate, material quality and drainage
explanation: Poor drainage is a leading cause of premature failure.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 6

topic: Design of flexible pavements as per IRC
stem: IRC 37 designs flexible pavements based on:
options: Cumulative standard axles and subgrade CBR
explanation: Design charts give total thickness and layer composition.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 6

topic: Design of flexible pavements as per IRC
stem: The design traffic in million standard axles is computed using:
options: Initial commercial traffic, growth rate, design life, vehicle damage factor and lane distribution factor
explanation: The growth is compounded over the design life.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 6

topic: Design of flexible pavements as per IRC
stem: The design life normally adopted for a new flexible national highway pavement is:
explanation: Rigid pavements are usually designed for 30 years.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 6

topic: Design of flexible pavements as per IRC
stem: If no growth rate data is available, IRC recommends an annual traffic growth rate of:
explanation: Actual growth should be obtained from traffic studies where possible.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 6

topic: Design of flexible pavements as per IRC
stem: The lane distribution factor for a two lane two way road as per IRC is:
options: 0.5 of total commercial vehicles in both directions
explanation: Each direction carries about half the commercial traffic.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 6

topic: Design of flexible pavements as per IRC
stem: The Group Index method of flexible pavement design uses:
options: Soil group index and traffic volume class to read total thickness
explanation: It is an empirical method now largely superseded.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 6

topic: Design of flexible pavements as per IRC
stem: A granular sub-base in flexible pavement primarily serves to:
options: Provide drainage and a working platform and distribute load to the subgrade
explanation: It also prevents intrusion of subgrade soil into the base.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 6

topic: Design of flexible pavements as per IRC
stem: A prime coat is applied:
options: Over a granular base to bond it with the overlying bituminous layer
explanation: A tack coat is used between two bituminous layers.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 6

topic: Rigid pavements: components, stresses and design
stem: Rigid pavements derive their load carrying capacity mainly from:
options: Flexural strength and slab action of the concrete
explanation: The concrete slab acts as a beam over the subgrade.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 6

topic: Rigid pavements: components, stresses and design
stem: Westergaard analysed rigid pavement slab stresses at:
options: Interior, edge and corner load positions
explanation: Corner loading generally gives the maximum stress.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 6

topic: Rigid pavements: components, stresses and design
stem: The radius of relative stiffness of a concrete slab depends on:
options: Slab modulus of elasticity, thickness, Poisson's ratio and modulus of subgrade reaction
explanation: It is denoted by l and appears in Westergaard's equations.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 6

topic: Rigid pavements: components, stresses and design
stem: Warping stresses in concrete pavements are caused by:
options: Temperature differential between the top and bottom of the slab
explanation: Bradbury's coefficients are used to compute them.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 6

topic: Rigid pavements: components, stresses and design
stem: Expansion joints in cement concrete pavements are provided to:
options: Allow the slab to expand during a temperature rise without buckling
explanation: Contraction joints relieve tensile stress due to shrinkage.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 6

topic: Rigid pavements: components, stresses and design
stem: Dowel bars in rigid pavements are provided to:
options: Transfer wheel load across a transverse joint while permitting movement
explanation: Tie bars, in contrast, hold longitudinal joints together.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 6

topic: Rigid pavements: components, stresses and design
stem: Tie bars in concrete pavements are:
options: Deformed bars across longitudinal joints preventing separation
Plain round bars across transverse joints
explanation: They are not load transfer devices.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 6

topic: Rigid pavements: components, stresses and design
stem: Frictional stresses in a concrete pavement arise due to:
options: Restraint offered by the subgrade to uniform slab expansion or contraction
explanation: They govern the spacing of contraction joints.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 6

topic: Rigid pavements: components, stresses and design
stem: A dry lean concrete sub-base under a concrete pavement provides:
options: A uniform firm support and prevents pumping of subgrade fines
explanation: It improves the effective modulus of subgrade reaction.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 6

topic: Rigid pavements: components, stresses and design
stem: Pumping in rigid pavements refers to:
options: Ejection of water and soil fines through joints under repeated loading
explanation: It leads to loss of support and corner cracking.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 6

topic: Rigid pavements: components, stresses and design
stem: Critical combination of stresses for rigid pavement design in summer at the edge is:
explanation: In winter at the corner, warping and load stresses may also combine.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 6

topic: Rigid pavements: components, stresses and design
stem: Continuously reinforced concrete pavement eliminates:
options: Transverse contraction joints by allowing closely spaced fine cracks
explanation: Steel holds the cracks tightly closed.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 6

topic: Design of flexible pavements as per IRC
stem: An overlay design determines:
options: Additional thickness required to strengthen an existing deficient pavement
explanation: Benkelman beam deflection studies are commonly used.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 6

topic: Rigid pavements: components, stresses and design
stem: Corner loading generally produces the maximum stress in a rigid pavement slab.
explanation: The slab is unsupported on two edges at the corner.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 6

stem: In a flexible pavement each successive lower layer may be weaker than the one above.
explanation: Stress reduces with depth, so lower layers need less strength.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 6

topic: Rigid pavements: components, stresses and design
stem:
Assertion (A): Dowel bars are plain round bars coated to allow slip.
Reason (R): They must transfer load while allowing the slab to expand and contract freely.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Bonding them would defeat the purpose of the expansion joint.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 6

topic: Design of flexible pavements as per IRC
stem:
Assertion (A): Cumulative standard axles are used instead of vehicle counts in pavement design.
Reason (R): Pavement damage is related to axle load raised approximately to the fourth power.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: A few heavy axles cause far more damage than many light vehicles.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 6

topic: Rigid pavements: components, stresses and design
stem: Which stresses are considered in rigid pavement design?
explanation: Marshall stability is a bituminous mix property.
source: BEU syllabus — Transportation Engineering, Unit 6

topic: Soil formation, types and scope of soil engineering
stem: Loess is a soil deposited by:
explanation: It is a uniformly graded silt sized aeolian deposit.
source: BEU syllabus — Geotechnical Engineering-I, Unit 1

topic: Soil formation, types and scope of soil engineering
stem: Alluvial soil is transported and deposited by:
explanation: Lacustrine soils are deposited in still lake water.
source: BEU syllabus — Geotechnical Engineering-I, Unit 1

topic: Soil formation, types and scope of soil engineering
stem: Soil mechanics is defined as the branch of science dealing with:
options: The behaviour of soil under stress and its engineering properties
explanation: Geotechnical engineering applies it to design of foundations and earthworks.
source: BEU syllabus — Geotechnical Engineering-I, Unit 1

topic: Soil formation, types and scope of soil engineering
stem: The main difference between soil and rock is that soil:
options: Has particles held together by weak inter-particle forces that can be separated by gentle mechanical means
explanation: Rock has strong permanent cohesive bonds between mineral grains.
source: BEU syllabus — Geotechnical Engineering-I, Unit 1

topic: Soil formation, types and scope of soil engineering
stem: The scope of soil engineering includes:
options: Foundation design, earth dams, retaining walls, pavements and slope stability
explanation: Soil is both a construction material and a foundation medium.
source: BEU syllabus — Geotechnical Engineering-I, Unit 1

topic: Soil formation, types and scope of soil engineering
stem: Black cotton soil is problematic in foundation engineering because it:
options: Swells on wetting and shrinks on drying
explanation: Montmorillonite is its dominant clay mineral.
source: BEU syllabus — Geotechnical Engineering-I, Unit 1

topic: Soil formation, types and scope of soil engineering
stem: Glacial till or moraine is characterised by:
options: A heterogeneous unsorted mixture of boulders, gravel, sand and clay
explanation: Glacial transport does not sort the material by size.
source: BEU syllabus — Geotechnical Engineering-I, Unit 1

topic: Three phase system and weight volume relationships
stem: Soil is regarded as a three phase system consisting of:
explanation: Fully saturated soil is a two phase system.
source: BEU syllabus — Geotechnical Engineering-I, Unit 1

topic: Three phase system and weight volume relationships
stem: Void ratio of a soil is defined as:
options: Volume of voids divided by volume of solids
Volume of water divided by voids
Volume of voids divided by total volume
Volume of air divided by voids
explanation: Porosity is the ratio of void volume to total volume.
source: BEU syllabus — Geotechnical Engineering-I, Unit 1

topic: Three phase system and weight volume relationships
stem: The relationship between void ratio e and porosity n is:
explanation: Conversely e equals n over (1 minus n).
source: BEU syllabus — Geotechnical Engineering-I, Unit 1

topic: Three phase system and weight volume relationships
stem: Degree of saturation is defined as:
options: Volume of water divided by total volume
Volume of water divided by volume of voids, expressed as a percentage
Weight of water divided by weight of solids
Volume of air divided by total volume
explanation: It equals 100 percent for fully saturated soil.
source: BEU syllabus — Geotechnical Engineering-I, Unit 1

topic: Three phase system and weight volume relationships
stem: Water content of a soil is defined as:
options: Weight of water divided by total weight
Weight of solids divided by weight of water
Volume of water divided by voids
Weight of water divided by weight of solids
explanation: It may exceed 100 percent for organic soils.
source: BEU syllabus — Geotechnical Engineering-I, Unit 1

topic: Three phase system and weight volume relationships
stem: The fundamental relation connecting e, w, G and S is:
explanation: For full saturation, e equals wG.
source: BEU syllabus — Geotechnical Engineering-I, Unit 1

topic: Three phase system and weight volume relationships
stem: Dry unit weight of a soil is related to bulk unit weight by:
explanation: Here w is the water content expressed as a fraction.
source: BEU syllabus — Geotechnical Engineering-I, Unit 1

topic: Three phase system and weight volume relationships
stem: Submerged unit weight of a soil equals:
options: Saturated unit weight minus the unit weight of water
explanation: It is used in effective stress computations below the water table.
source: BEU syllabus — Geotechnical Engineering-I, Unit 1

topic: Three phase system and weight volume relationships
stem: Specific gravity of soil solids for most inorganic soils lies between:
explanation: It is determined using a pycnometer or density bottle.
source: BEU syllabus — Geotechnical Engineering-I, Unit 1

topic: Three phase system and weight volume relationships
stem: Percentage air voids in a soil is given by:
explanation: It vanishes when the soil is fully saturated.
source: BEU syllabus — Geotechnical Engineering-I, Unit 1

topic: Three phase system and weight volume relationships
stem: Relative density of a cohesionless soil is expressed in terms of:
options: Maximum, minimum and natural void ratios
explanation: A value above 70 percent indicates a dense sand.
source: BEU syllabus — Geotechnical Engineering-I, Unit 1

stem: The liquid limit of a soil is the water content at which soil changes from:
options: The solid to the semi-solid state
The plastic state to the liquid state
explanation: It is determined by the Casagrande apparatus or cone penetrometer.
source: BEU syllabus — Geotechnical Engineering-I, Unit 1

stem: Plasticity index is defined as:
options: Liquid limit divided by plastic limit
explanation: It indicates the range of water content over which soil is plastic.
source: BEU syllabus — Geotechnical Engineering-I, Unit 1

stem: The plastic limit is determined by rolling a soil thread to a diameter of:
explanation: The thread just begins to crumble at this diameter.
source: BEU syllabus — Geotechnical Engineering-I, Unit 1

stem: In the Casagrande liquid limit test, the groove closes over a length of 12.5 mm at:
explanation: A flow curve of water content versus log of blows is plotted.
source: BEU syllabus — Geotechnical Engineering-I, Unit 1

stem: Shrinkage limit is the water content at which:
options: Further loss of water causes no further reduction in volume
explanation: The soil remains saturated at the shrinkage limit.
source: BEU syllabus — Geotechnical Engineering-I, Unit 1

stem: The uniformity coefficient of a soil is defined as:
explanation: A value greater than 4 for gravel indicates well graded soil.
source: BEU syllabus — Geotechnical Engineering-I, Unit 1

stem: The coefficient of curvature is given by:
explanation: A value between 1 and 3 indicates good gradation.
source: BEU syllabus — Geotechnical Engineering-I, Unit 1

stem: In the Indian Standard soil classification system, the symbol CH denotes:
explanation: Liquid limit greater than 50 defines high compressibility.
source: BEU syllabus — Geotechnical Engineering-I, Unit 1

stem: The A-line on the plasticity chart separates:
options: Clays lying above from silts and organic soils lying below
explanation: Its equation is Ip equals 0.73 times (wL minus 20).
source: BEU syllabus — Geotechnical Engineering-I, Unit 1

stem: Sedimentation analysis using the hydrometer is based on:

explanation: It is used for particles finer than 75 microns.
source: BEU syllabus — Geotechnical Engineering-I, Unit 1

topic: Three phase system and weight volume relationships
stem: For a fully saturated soil, the void ratio equals the product of water content and specific gravity.
explanation: This follows from the relation Se equals wG with S equal to unity.
source: BEU syllabus — Geotechnical Engineering-I, Unit 1

stem: Plasticity index equals the liquid limit minus the shrinkage limit.
explanation: It is the liquid limit minus the plastic limit.
source: BEU syllabus — Geotechnical Engineering-I, Unit 1

topic: Soil formation, types and scope of soil engineering
stem:
Assertion (A): Black cotton soil is unsuitable as a foundation medium without treatment.
Reason (R): It undergoes large volume changes with seasonal variation of moisture content.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Under-reamed piles or soil replacement are common remedies.
source: BEU syllabus — Geotechnical Engineering-I, Unit 1

stem:
Assertion (A): Atterberg limits are determined on the fraction passing the 425 micron sieve.
Reason (R): Plasticity is a property of the fine grained portion of the soil.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Coarse particles would disturb the test result.
source: BEU syllabus — Geotechnical Engineering-I, Unit 1

topic: Three phase system and weight volume relationships
stem: Which of the following are volumetric relationships of soil?
explanation: Liquid limit is an index property expressed as a water content.
source: BEU syllabus — Geotechnical Engineering-I, Unit 1

stem: The boundary layer concept was first introduced by:
explanation: Prandtl proposed it in 1904 for flow of real fluids past a body.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 1

stem: Boundary layer thickness is conventionally defined as the distance from the boundary where the velocity reaches:
options: 99 percent of the free stream velocity
explanation: Velocity approaches the free stream value asymptotically.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 1

stem: Displacement thickness represents the distance by which the boundary is displaced to account for:
options: The reduction in mass flow rate due to the boundary layer
explanation: It is the integral of (1 minus u over U) across the layer.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 1

stem: Momentum thickness accounts for:
options: The loss of momentum flux in the boundary layer
explanation: It equals the integral of (u/U)(1 minus u/U) dy.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 1

stem: Energy thickness is defined by the integral of:
explanation: It represents the loss of kinetic energy flux.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 1

stem: Shape factor of a boundary layer is the ratio of:
explanation: Its value indicates the proximity to separation.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 1

stem: The key assumption of boundary layer theory is that:
options: Viscous effects are confined to a thin layer near the boundary and pressure is constant across it
Pressure varies strongly across the layer
explanation: Outside the layer the flow may be treated as ideal.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 1

stem: The von Karman momentum integral equation relates the wall shear stress to:
options: The rate of change of momentum thickness along the plate
explanation: It gives tau0 equal to rho U squared times d theta by dx.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 1

topic: Laminar and turbulent boundary layers on a flat plate
stem: On a flat plate, the boundary layer is normally laminar up to a Reynolds number of about:
explanation: Beyond this the layer becomes turbulent.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 1

topic: Laminar and turbulent boundary layers on a flat plate
stem: According to Blasius, the laminar boundary layer thickness on a flat plate varies as:
explanation: It therefore grows as the square root of the distance x.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 1

topic: Laminar and turbulent boundary layers on a flat plate
stem: For a turbulent boundary layer on a smooth flat plate, thickness varies approximately as:
explanation: It grows faster than the laminar layer, roughly as x to the four fifths.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 1

topic: Laminar and turbulent boundary layers on a flat plate
stem: The laminar sub-layer is:
options: A very thin viscous layer next to a smooth wall inside a turbulent boundary layer
explanation: Its thickness decreases as Reynolds number increases.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 1

topic: Laminar and turbulent boundary layers on a flat plate
stem: A boundary is said to be hydrodynamically smooth when:
options: The average roughness height is much less than the laminar sub-layer thickness
explanation: Roughness projections are then submerged in the viscous sub-layer.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 1

topic: Laminar and turbulent boundary layers on a flat plate
stem: The local skin friction coefficient for laminar flow over a flat plate is:
explanation: The average coefficient over length L is 1.328 over root Re L.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 1

topic: Laminar and turbulent boundary layers on a flat plate
stem: The average drag coefficient for laminar flow over the whole plate of length L is:
explanation: It is exactly twice the local value at x equal to L.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 1

topic: Laminar and turbulent boundary layers on a flat plate
stem: For turbulent flow over a smooth plate, the average drag coefficient for Re between 5e5 and 1e7 is:
explanation: Turbulent drag is much higher than laminar at the same Reynolds number.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 1

topic: Laminar and turbulent boundary layers on a flat plate
stem: The one seventh power law velocity profile is applicable to:
options: Turbulent boundary layers on smooth plates at moderate Reynolds numbers
explanation: It gives u over U equal to (y over delta) to the power one seventh.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 1

stem: Boundary layer separation occurs when:
options: An adverse pressure gradient causes the velocity gradient at the wall to become zero
explanation: Beyond that point reverse flow begins.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 1

stem: The condition at the point of separation is:
explanation: A negative value indicates the flow has already separated.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 1

stem: An adverse pressure gradient is characterised by:
options: Pressure increasing in the direction of flow
explanation: It decelerates the fluid near the wall and promotes separation.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 1

stem: Which of the following is a method of controlling boundary layer separation?
options: Reducing the free stream velocity to zero
Suction of the low energy fluid through slots
explanation: Blowing high energy fluid and streamlining are other methods.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 1

stem: Streamlining a body reduces:
options: Pressure drag by delaying or preventing separation
explanation: A streamlined body has a gradual rear taper.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 1

stem: Total drag on a body immersed in a real fluid is the sum of:
options: Skin friction drag and pressure or form drag
explanation: Form drag dominates for bluff bodies.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 1

stem: A turbulent boundary layer resists separation better than a laminar one because:
options: It has greater momentum near the wall due to turbulent mixing
explanation: This is why golf balls are dimpled.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 1

stem: The wake behind a bluff body is:
options: The region of separated, low pressure, turbulent flow downstream
explanation: Its size determines the pressure drag.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 1

stem: Boundary layer suction control is achieved by:
options: Removing the retarded fluid through perforations in the surface
explanation: It restores the velocity profile and delays separation.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 1

stem: Inside the boundary layer, the pressure across its thickness is assumed:
options: Constant and equal to the free stream pressure at that section
explanation: The layer is very thin compared with body dimensions.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 1

stem: For a linear velocity distribution u/U equal to y/delta, the displacement thickness is:
explanation: Momentum thickness for the same profile is delta by 6.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 1

topic: Laminar and turbulent boundary layers on a flat plate
stem: The Blasius solution applies to:
options: Steady laminar boundary layer flow over a flat plate with zero pressure gradient
explanation: It reduces the partial differential equations to an ordinary one.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 1

stem: Separation cannot occur when the pressure gradient is favourable.
explanation: A favourable gradient accelerates the near wall fluid and keeps the flow attached.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 1

stem: Displacement thickness is always greater than momentum thickness for a given profile.
explanation: Hence the shape factor is greater than unity.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 1

topic: Laminar and turbulent boundary layers on a flat plate
stem:
Assertion (A): Dimples on a golf ball reduce the total drag.
Reason (R): They trigger a turbulent boundary layer which resists separation and shrinks the wake.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: The reduction in pressure drag outweighs the increase in skin friction.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 1

topic: Laminar and turbulent boundary layers on a flat plate
stem:
Assertion (A): Laminar sub-layer thickness decreases with increasing Reynolds number.
Reason (R): Higher velocities produce steeper velocity gradients near the wall.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: A pipe may therefore behave as rough at high Reynolds numbers.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 1

stem: Which of the following are boundary layer thickness measures?
explanation: Hydraulic radius is an open channel geometry parameter.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 1

topic: Comparison of open channel flow and pipe flow
stem: The essential distinguishing feature of open channel flow is:
