explanation: Pipe flow may be full and under pressure with no free surface.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 2

topic: Comparison of open channel flow and pipe flow
stem: The driving force for flow in an open channel is:
options: The component of gravity along the channel slope
explanation: Pipe flow is driven mainly by a pressure gradient.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 2

topic: Comparison of open channel flow and pipe flow
stem: The hydraulic grade line in open channel flow coincides with:
explanation: In pipe flow it lies above the pipe axis by the pressure head.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 2

topic: Comparison of open channel flow and pipe flow
stem: Compared with pipe flow, open channel flow analysis is more complex because:
options: The free surface position is itself unknown and varies with flow
explanation: Cross sectional area therefore depends on depth.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 2

topic: Comparison of open channel flow and pipe flow
stem: The important dimensionless number governing open channel flow is:
explanation: It expresses the ratio of inertia to gravity forces.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 2

topic: Comparison of open channel flow and pipe flow
stem: A partially filled sewer pipe is an example of:
explanation: It has a free surface even though the conduit is closed.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 2

topic: Geometrical parameters and classification of channels
stem: Hydraulic radius of a channel section is defined as:

topic: Geometrical parameters and classification of channels
stem: Hydraulic depth of a channel section is:

explanation: It is used in computing the Froude number.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 2

topic: Geometrical parameters and classification of channels
stem: A prismatic channel is one in which:

explanation: Natural rivers are generally non-prismatic.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 2

topic: Geometrical parameters and classification of channels
stem: Open channels are classified as natural and artificial; an example of an artificial channel is:
explanation: Artificial channels have regular geometry and known roughness.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 2

topic: Geometrical parameters and classification of channels
stem: Section factor for critical flow computation is defined as:
options: Area times the square root of hydraulic depth
explanation: It is written as Z equal to A root of (A over T).
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 2

topic: Geometrical parameters and classification of channels
stem: A rigid boundary channel is one in which:

explanation: Alluvial channels have mobile boundaries.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 2

topic: Geometrical parameters and classification of channels
stem: For a trapezoidal channel of bottom width b, depth y and side slope m horizontal to 1 vertical, the flow area is:

source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 2

topic: Geometrical parameters and classification of channels
stem: A channel is described as wide rectangular when:

source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 2

topic: Classification of open channel flow and velocity distribution
stem: Steady flow in an open channel means:

Flow parameters at a section do not change with time
explanation: Uniform flow means no change with distance.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 2

topic: Classification of open channel flow and velocity distribution
stem: Uniform flow in an open channel occurs when:
options: Depth, area and velocity remain constant along the channel length
explanation: The water surface is then parallel to the bed.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 2

topic: Classification of open channel flow and velocity distribution
stem: Gradually varied flow is a:

explanation: Curvature of the streamlines is negligible.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 2

topic: Classification of open channel flow and velocity distribution
stem: A hydraulic jump is an example of:

source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 2

topic: Classification of open channel flow and velocity distribution

source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 2

topic: Classification of open channel flow and velocity distribution
stem: At critical flow, the Froude number equals:
explanation: Specific energy is a minimum for a given discharge.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 2

topic: Classification of open channel flow and velocity distribution
stem: In supercritical flow, a surface disturbance:
explanation: Flow velocity exceeds the wave celerity.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 2

topic: Classification of open channel flow and velocity distribution

source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 2

topic: Classification of open channel flow and velocity distribution
stem: In a wide open channel, the maximum velocity generally occurs:

source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 2

topic: Classification of open channel flow and velocity distribution
stem: The mean velocity in a channel is approximately equal to the velocity measured at a depth of:

topic: Classification of open channel flow and velocity distribution
stem: The energy correction factor alpha for a channel section is:

topic: Classification of open channel flow and velocity distribution
stem: The velocity distribution in a turbulent open channel flow is well described by:
explanation: Laminar channel flow, by contrast, gives a parabolic profile.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 2

topic: Classification of open channel flow and velocity distribution
stem: Spatially varied flow refers to a flow in which:

source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 2

topic: Classification of open channel flow and velocity distribution
stem: Unsteady non-uniform flow occurs in a channel during:

source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 2

topic: Comparison of open channel flow and pipe flow

source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 2

topic: Geometrical parameters and classification of channels
stem: Hydraulic radius equals the depth for a wide rectangular channel.

source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 2

topic: Classification of open channel flow and velocity distribution
stem:
Assertion (A): Control of subcritical flow lies downstream.

options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Supercritical flow is controlled from upstream.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 2

topic: Comparison of open channel flow and pipe flow
stem:
Assertion (A): The free surface makes open channel flow analysis more difficult than pipe flow.

options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Iterative or trial solutions are therefore common.

topic: Classification of open channel flow and velocity distribution
stem: Which of the following are classifications of open channel flow?

topic: Continuity, energy and momentum equations; uniform flow
stem: The average boundary shear stress in uniform flow is given by:

topic: Continuity, energy and momentum equations; uniform flow
stem: Total energy per unit weight at a channel section is:

stem: Characteristics of uniform flow include:

explanation: It can occur only in long prismatic channels.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 3

stem: Chezy's formula for mean velocity in uniform flow is:
explanation: C is Chezy's coefficient with dimensions of root length per time.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 3

topic: Chezy and Manning formulae and roughness
stem: Manning's formula for mean velocity is:

topic: Chezy and Manning formulae and roughness
stem: The relation between Chezy's C and Manning's n is:

source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 3

topic: Chezy and Manning formulae and roughness
stem: A typical value of Manning's n for a smooth cement lined channel is about:

topic: Most economical channel section and normal depth
stem: A channel section is said to be most economical when for a given area it has:
options: The minimum wetted perimeter and hence maximum discharge
explanation: It also corresponds to the minimum lining cost.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 3

topic: Most economical channel section and normal depth
stem: For the most economical rectangular channel section:
options: The width equals twice the depth
explanation: The hydraulic radius is then half the depth.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 3

topic: Most economical channel section and normal depth
stem: For the most economical trapezoidal section, the hydraulic radius equals:
explanation: A semicircle can be inscribed in the section with centre on the water surface.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 3

topic: Most economical channel section and normal depth
stem: The most economical trapezoidal section has a side slope corresponding to:
explanation: The best side slope is 1 horizontal to root 3 vertical.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 3

topic: Most economical channel section and normal depth
stem: Normal depth is the depth of flow:
options: At which specific energy is minimum
At which uniform flow occurs for a given discharge, slope and roughness
explanation: It is obtained by trial from Manning's equation.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 3

topic: Most economical channel section and normal depth
stem: For a circular channel, maximum discharge occurs at a depth of about:
explanation: Maximum velocity occurs at about 0.81 times the diameter.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 3

topic: Most economical channel section and normal depth
stem: The most economical section of all shapes for a given area is:
explanation: It has the smallest perimeter for a given area.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 3

topic: Specific energy, critical flow and discharge measurement
stem: Specific energy of a channel section is the energy measured with respect to:
explanation: It equals depth plus velocity head.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 3

topic: Specific energy, critical flow and discharge measurement
stem: For a given specific energy, the specific energy curve shows:
options: Two alternate depths, one subcritical and one supercritical
explanation: They coincide at the critical depth where energy is minimum.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 3

topic: Specific energy, critical flow and discharge measurement
stem: Critical depth for a rectangular channel with discharge per unit width q is:
explanation: Minimum specific energy equals 1.5 times the critical depth.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 3

topic: Specific energy, critical flow and discharge measurement
stem: At critical depth in a rectangular channel, the velocity head equals:
explanation: Hence minimum specific energy equals three halves of yc.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 3

topic: Specific energy, critical flow and discharge measurement
stem: Specific force is the sum of:
options: The momentum flux and the pressure force per unit weight at a section
explanation: Its minimum also occurs at the critical depth.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 3

topic: Specific energy, critical flow and discharge measurement
stem: A Venturi flume measures discharge by:
options: Contracting the channel width and measuring depths upstream and at the throat
explanation: It causes little head loss compared with a weir.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 3

topic: Specific energy, critical flow and discharge measurement
stem: A standing wave flume differs from a Venturi flume in that:
options: It creates critical flow at the throat so only the upstream depth is needed
explanation: A hydraulic jump forms downstream of the throat.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 3

topic: Specific energy, critical flow and discharge measurement
stem: A current meter measures:
options: Point velocity in a channel from the rotation of a cup or propeller
explanation: The area velocity method then gives discharge.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 3

topic: Specific energy, critical flow and discharge measurement
stem: A channel transition such as a hump raised in subcritical flow causes the water surface to:
explanation: In supercritical flow the surface rises over a hump.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 3

topic: Specific energy, critical flow and discharge measurement
stem: Critical depth in a channel is independent of:
explanation: It depends only on discharge and section shape.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 3

topic: Most economical channel section and normal depth
stem: For a most economical rectangular channel the hydraulic radius equals half the depth.
explanation: This follows from the condition that width equals twice the depth.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 3

topic: Chezy and Manning formulae and roughness
stem: Manning's n increases as the channel surface becomes smoother.
explanation: Smoother surfaces have lower values of n.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 3

topic: Specific energy, critical flow and discharge measurement
stem:
Assertion (A): Specific energy is minimum at the critical depth.
Reason (R): Differentiating the specific energy expression with respect to depth and equating to zero gives the critical condition.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: The corresponding Froude number is unity.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 3

topic: Most economical channel section and normal depth
stem:
Assertion (A): The semicircular section is hydraulically the most efficient shape.
Reason (R): For a given flow area, the semicircle has the least wetted perimeter.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Practical construction difficulties often favour trapezoidal sections.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 3

topic: Chezy and Manning formulae and roughness
stem: Which factors affect Manning's roughness coefficient n?
explanation: Temperature has a negligible effect in fully turbulent channel flow.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 3

topic: Theory and elements of the hydraulic jump
stem: A hydraulic jump occurs when flow changes from:
explanation: It is accompanied by a sudden rise in depth and loss of energy.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 4

topic: Theory and elements of the hydraulic jump
stem: The analysis of a hydraulic jump is based on:
explanation: Energy loss in the jump is initially unknown.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 4

topic: Theory and elements of the hydraulic jump
stem: The two depths on either side of a hydraulic jump are called:
explanation: Alternate depths, in contrast, have equal specific energy.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 4

topic: Theory and elements of the hydraulic jump
stem: For a rectangular channel, the sequent depth ratio is:
explanation: F1 is the Froude number of the incoming supercritical flow.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 4

topic: Theory and elements of the hydraulic jump
stem: The energy loss in a hydraulic jump in a rectangular channel is:
explanation: It is dissipated mainly as turbulence and heat.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 4

topic: Theory and elements of the hydraulic jump
stem: The height of a hydraulic jump is:
options: The difference between the sequent depths
explanation: Length of the jump is typically 5 to 7 times the height.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 4

topic: Theory and elements of the hydraulic jump
stem: Specific force before and after a hydraulic jump is:
explanation: This equality forms the basis of the jump equation.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 4

topic: Theory and elements of the hydraulic jump
stem: The length of a hydraulic jump is usually determined from:
options: Empirical curves relating L to y2 and the initial Froude number
explanation: Theoretical prediction of the jump length is not possible.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 4

topic: Theory and elements of the hydraulic jump
stem: The efficiency of a hydraulic jump is the ratio of:
options: Specific energy after the jump to that before the jump
Energy loss to the initial energy
explanation: Efficiency decreases as the initial Froude number increases.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 4

topic: Types, location and applications of the jump
stem: A jump with an incoming Froude number between 1.0 and 1.7 is called:
explanation: The surface shows undulations with very little energy loss.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 4

topic: Types, location and applications of the jump
stem: A jump with Froude number between 4.5 and 9.0 is classified as:
explanation: It is well balanced and gives 45 to 70 percent energy dissipation.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 4

topic: Types, location and applications of the jump
stem: A jump with Froude number greater than 9.0 is called:
explanation: It dissipates up to 85 percent of the energy but is rough.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 4

topic: Types, location and applications of the jump
stem: An oscillating jump, with Froude number between 2.5 and 4.5, is undesirable because:
options: It generates surface waves that travel far downstream
explanation: Wave suppressors may be required.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 4

topic: Types, location and applications of the jump
stem: The most important practical application of the hydraulic jump is:
options: Dissipation of energy downstream of spillways and sluice gates
explanation: It protects the downstream bed from scour.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 4

topic: Types, location and applications of the jump
stem: A stilling basin is designed to:
options: Confine the hydraulic jump within a protected apron
explanation: Baffle blocks and end sills stabilise the jump.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 4

topic: Types, location and applications of the jump
stem: Other uses of the hydraulic jump include:
options: Mixing chemicals in water treatment and aerating water
explanation: The intense turbulence promotes rapid mixing.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 4

topic: Types, location and applications of the jump
stem: A repelled jump occurs when:
options: The tailwater depth is less than the required sequent depth
explanation: The jump moves downstream away from the structure.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 4

topic: Types, location and applications of the jump
stem: A submerged or drowned jump results when:
options: The tailwater depth exceeds the sequent depth
Tailwater is less than the sequent depth
explanation: Energy dissipation is then reduced.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 4

topic: Types, location and applications of the jump
stem: For efficient energy dissipation, the ideal situation is when:
options: The tailwater depth exactly equals the sequent depth
explanation: The jump then forms at the toe of the structure.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 4

topic: Types, location and applications of the jump
stem: A jump on a sloping channel bed differs from one on a horizontal bed because:
options: The weight component along the flow must be included in the momentum equation
explanation: Sequent depth ratios therefore differ from the classical formula.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 4

stem: A surge in an open channel is:
options: A moving wave front produced by a sudden change in flow
explanation: It may be treated as a moving hydraulic jump.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 4

stem: A positive surge is one in which:
options: The depth increases behind the advancing wave front
explanation: A negative surge involves a fall in depth.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 4

stem: Sudden closure of a gate in a canal produces:
explanation: Sudden opening produces a negative surge moving downstream.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 4

stem: A surge is analysed by:
options: Superimposing the surge velocity so that the flow becomes steady relative to the wave
explanation: The standard jump equations then apply in the moving frame.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 4

stem: The celerity of a small amplitude gravity wave in shallow water is:
explanation: The Froude number compares flow velocity with this celerity.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 4

stem: A negative surge is unstable in shape because:
options: Points of greater depth travel faster, causing the wave to flatten
explanation: A positive surge, in contrast, tends to steepen and remain stable.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 4

stem: A tidal bore in an estuary is an example of:
explanation: It forms when the tidal range is large and the estuary funnel shaped.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 4

topic: Theory and elements of the hydraulic jump
stem: Immediately upstream of a hydraulic jump the flow is:
options: Shallow and fast with a Froude number greater than one
explanation: Downstream the flow is deep, slow and subcritical.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 4

topic: Types, location and applications of the jump
stem: The location of a hydraulic jump downstream of a sluice gate is determined by:
options: Matching the sequent depth with the tailwater depth using gradually varied flow profiles
explanation: The M3 profile downstream of the gate is computed first.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 4

topic: Theory and elements of the hydraulic jump
stem: A hydraulic jump always involves a loss of energy.
explanation: Turbulence and eddies dissipate a substantial part of the incoming energy.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 4

topic: Types, location and applications of the jump
stem: A submerged jump dissipates more energy than a free jump.
explanation: Excess tailwater drowns the jump and reduces dissipation efficiency.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 4

topic: Theory and elements of the hydraulic jump
stem:
Assertion (A): The momentum equation, not the energy equation, is used to analyse a hydraulic jump.
Reason (R): The energy loss across the jump is not known in advance.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: The external forces on the control volume are, however, computable.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 4

stem:
Assertion (A): A positive surge tends to steepen as it advances.
Reason (R): Greater depths travel with higher celerity and overtake the shallower front.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Eventually it forms a moving hydraulic jump.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 4

topic: Types, location and applications of the jump
stem: Which of the following are practical applications of the hydraulic jump?
explanation: Rainfall measurement uses rain gauges, not hydraulic jumps.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 4

stem: The three governing conservation principles of computational fluid dynamics are conservation of:
explanation: They yield the continuity, Navier Stokes and energy equations.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 5

stem: The Navier Stokes equations express:
options: Conservation of momentum for a viscous fluid
explanation: They are non-linear partial differential equations.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 5

stem: The continuity equation for an incompressible flow reduces to:
options: Divergence of the velocity vector equals zero
explanation: Density is constant so the time derivative term vanishes.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 5

stem: The Euler equations are obtained from the Navier Stokes equations by:
explanation: They describe inviscid or ideal fluid flow.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 5

stem: For inviscid incompressible irrotational flow, the velocity potential satisfies:
explanation: Potential flow theory then applies.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 5

stem: The substantial or material derivative represents:
options: The rate of change following a fluid particle, combining local and convective terms
explanation: It links the Lagrangian and Eulerian descriptions.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 5

stem: The shallow water equations used in river modelling are also known as:
explanation: They comprise a continuity and a momentum equation in one dimension.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 5

stem: Reynolds averaged Navier Stokes modelling requires a turbulence closure because:
options: Averaging introduces unknown Reynolds stress terms
explanation: Models such as k-epsilon supply the closure.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 5

stem: Grid generation in CFD refers to:
options: Discretising the flow domain into a set of cells or elements
explanation: Grid quality strongly influences solution accuracy.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 5

stem: A structured grid is one in which:
options: Cells are arranged in a regular indexed pattern
explanation: Unstructured grids permit arbitrary connectivity and complex geometry.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 5

stem: The finite volume method is popular in CFD because:
options: It conserves fluxes exactly over each control volume
explanation: Conservation is satisfied both locally and globally.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 5

stem: The finite difference method approximates derivatives by:
options: Truncated Taylor series expansions at grid points
explanation: It is simplest on structured rectangular grids.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 5

stem: The Courant number condition in explicit schemes requires that:
options: The time step be small enough that information does not cross more than one cell
explanation: It is a necessary condition for numerical stability.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 5

stem: Grid independence study in CFD is performed to:
options: Confirm that the solution does not change appreciably on further grid refinement
explanation: It is an essential part of solution verification.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 5

stem: Boundary layer resolution in a CFD mesh requires:
options: Fine clustering of cells normal to the wall
explanation: The wall y plus value guides the near wall spacing.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 5

stem: Numerical diffusion in CFD arises mainly from:
options: Low order upwind discretisation of convective terms
explanation: It artificially smears sharp gradients.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 5

stem: An implicit time marching scheme is preferred when:
options: Large time steps are required and stability limits explicit schemes
explanation: It requires solving a system of equations each step.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 5

stem: Verification in CFD differs from validation in that verification checks:
options: Whether the equations are solved correctly, while validation checks the right equations were solved
explanation: Validation compares results with physical measurements.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 5

stem: Hydroinformatics may be defined as:
options: The application of information and communication technology to water related problems
explanation: It integrates modelling, data and decision support.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 5

stem: A decision support system in water resources typically combines:
options: Models, databases and a user interface to aid management decisions
explanation: It supports rather than replaces the decision maker.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 5

stem: Geographic information systems are used in water resources engineering to:
options: Store, analyse and display spatially referenced hydrological data
explanation: Watershed delineation from digital elevation models is a common application.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 5

stem: Remote sensing data is useful in hydrology for estimating:
options: Land use, snow cover, soil moisture and rainfall distribution
explanation: Satellite imagery provides wide areal coverage.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 5

stem: Web based modelling in water resources allows:
options: Remote access to models and data through a browser without local installation
explanation: It facilitates collaboration among distributed stakeholders.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 5

stem: Artificial neural networks in hydroinformatics are commonly used for:
options: Rainfall runoff modelling and flow forecasting from historical data
explanation: They are data driven rather than physically based models.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 5

stem: SCADA systems in water supply networks are used for:
options: Supervisory control and real time data acquisition from remote sites
explanation: They enable remote monitoring of pressures and flows.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 5

stem: A digital twin of a water distribution network refers to:
options: A continuously updated virtual model mirroring the real system using live data
explanation: It supports predictive operation and maintenance.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 5

stem: A major limitation of data driven models such as neural networks is that they:
options: Extrapolate poorly beyond the range of the training data
explanation: Physically based models are preferred for extreme events.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 5

stem: Commonly used CFD software for hydraulic engineering problems includes:
explanation: HEC-RAS and MIKE are used for one dimensional river modelling.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 5

stem: An inviscid incompressible flow assumption is reasonable when:
options: Viscous effects are confined to thin boundary layers and Mach number is low
explanation: It permits potential flow solutions outside the boundary layer.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 5

stem: A finer computational grid always guarantees a more accurate CFD result.
explanation: Accuracy also depends on the physical models, boundary conditions and discretisation scheme.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 5

stem: The Navier Stokes equations are non-linear partial differential equations.
explanation: The convective acceleration term makes them non-linear.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 5

stem:
Assertion (A): The finite volume method is widely used in hydraulic CFD.

Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A

stem:
Assertion (A): Hydroinformatics has grown rapidly in recent decades.
Reason (R): Cheap computing power, sensors and internet connectivity have become widely available.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: This has enabled real time monitoring and modelling of water systems.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering, Unit 5

stem: The horizontal thrust in a two hinged parabolic arch under a uniformly distributed load over the whole span is:

topic: Flexibility coefficients and unit load method
stem: The consistent deformation method is another name for:

stem: A statically determinate structure develops stresses due to temperature change.

unit_title: Analysis of indeterminate structures by force methods Flexibility coefficients Unit
topic: Flexibility coefficients and unit load method
stem:
Assertion (A): The flexibility matrix of a linear elastic structure is symmetric.
Reason (R): Maxwell's reciprocal theorem states that the deflection at A due to unit load at B equals that at B due to unit load at A.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Symmetry reduces the computational work considerably.
source: BEU syllabus — Structural Analysis, Unit 1

unit_title: Analysis of indeterminate structures by force methods Flexibility coefficients Unit
stem:
Assertion (A): Influence lines are indispensable in bridge girder design.
Reason (R): Bridge loads are moving loads whose critical positions must be located.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Static analysis at a fixed load position would be inadequate.
source: BEU syllabus — Structural Analysis, Unit 1

unit_title: Analysis of indeterminate structures by force methods Flexibility coefficients Unit

explanation: Moment distribution is a displacement or stiffness based method.

unit_title: Energy Methods: Principle of minimum potential energy Principle of virtual

stem: Total potential energy of a structure is the sum of:

explanation: It is stationary for equilibrium configurations.

unit_title: Energy Methods: Principle of minimum potential energy Principle of virtual

unit_title: Energy Methods: Principle of minimum potential energy Principle of virtual

stem: Complementary strain energy for a linear elastic material is:

unit_title: Energy Methods: Principle of minimum potential energy Principle of virtual

stem: Strain energy due to torsion in a shaft is:

source: BEU syllabus — Structural Analysis, Unit 2

unit_title: Energy Methods: Principle of minimum potential energy Principle of virtual
topic: Strain energy and principle of minimum potential energy
stem: Resilience of a material is defined as:
options: The strain energy stored up to the elastic limit
explanation: Modulus of resilience is resilience per unit volume.
source: BEU syllabus — Structural Analysis, Unit 2

unit_title: Energy Methods: Principle of minimum potential energy Principle of virtual
topic: Strain energy and principle of minimum potential energy
stem: For a suddenly applied load, the instantaneous stress produced is:

source: BEU syllabus — Structural Analysis, Unit 2

unit_title: Energy Methods: Principle of minimum potential energy Principle of virtual
topic: Strain energy and principle of minimum potential energy
stem: The principle of stationary potential energy applied to a structure yields:
options: The equilibrium equations of the system
explanation: It is a variational statement of equilibrium.
source: BEU syllabus — Structural Analysis, Unit 2

unit_title: Energy Methods: Principle of minimum potential energy Principle of virtual
stem: The principle of virtual work states that for a body in equilibrium:
options: The total virtual work done by all forces during a virtual displacement is zero
explanation: External virtual work equals internal virtual work.
source: BEU syllabus — Structural Analysis, Unit 2

unit_title: Energy Methods: Principle of minimum potential energy Principle of virtual
stem: A virtual displacement must be:
options: Small and compatible with the constraints of the structure
explanation: It need not actually occur in the structure.
source: BEU syllabus — Structural Analysis, Unit 2

unit_title: Energy Methods: Principle of minimum potential energy Principle of virtual
stem: The method of virtual work used with a unit virtual load is known as:
options: The unit load method or dummy load method
explanation: It is used to compute deflections and rotations.
source: BEU syllabus — Structural Analysis, Unit 2

unit_title: Energy Methods: Principle of minimum potential energy Principle of virtual
stem: In the principle of virtual forces, one applies:
options: A virtual force system in equilibrium to real compatible deformations
explanation: It is used to compute displacements.
source: BEU syllabus — Structural Analysis, Unit 2

unit_title: Energy Methods: Principle of minimum potential energy Principle of virtual
stem: The Rayleigh Ritz method is based on:

explanation: It gives an upper bound to the stiffness of the system.
source: BEU syllabus — Structural Analysis, Unit 2

unit_title: Energy Methods: Principle of minimum potential energy Principle of virtual
stem: The unit load method applied to a rigid frame with axial, shear and bending effects usually neglects:
options: Axial and shear strain energy compared with bending
explanation: For slender members bending dominates the deflection.
source: BEU syllabus — Structural Analysis, Unit 2

unit_title: Energy Methods: Principle of minimum potential energy Principle of virtual
stem: Virtual work methods are applicable to:
options: Both statically determinate and indeterminate structures
explanation: They form the basis of most modern matrix methods.
source: BEU syllabus — Structural Analysis, Unit 2

unit_title: Energy Methods: Principle of minimum potential energy Principle of virtual

unit_title: Energy Methods: Principle of minimum potential energy Principle of virtual

explanation: It applies to linear elastic structures.
source: BEU syllabus — Structural Analysis, Unit 2

unit_title: Energy Methods: Principle of minimum potential energy Principle of virtual
stem: For a beam, Castigliano's second theorem gives deflection as:
explanation: P is the load at the point where deflection is required.
source: BEU syllabus — Structural Analysis, Unit 2

unit_title: Energy Methods: Principle of minimum potential energy Principle of virtual
stem: If no load exists at the point where deflection is required, Castigliano's method uses:
options: A fictitious load which is set to zero after differentiation
explanation: This is called the dummy load technique.
source: BEU syllabus — Structural Analysis, Unit 2

unit_title: Energy Methods: Principle of minimum potential energy Principle of virtual
stem: The theorem of least work states that redundant forces in a structure take values that:
options: Make the total strain energy a minimum
explanation: It is a corollary of Castigliano's second theorem.
source: BEU syllabus — Structural Analysis, Unit 2

unit_title: Energy Methods: Principle of minimum potential energy Principle of virtual
stem: Maxwell's reciprocal theorem states that:
options: Deflection at A due to a unit load at B equals deflection at B due to a unit load at A
explanation: It applies to linear elastic structures.
source: BEU syllabus — Structural Analysis, Unit 2

unit_title: Energy Methods: Principle of minimum potential energy Principle of virtual
stem: Betti's theorem is a generalisation of:

explanation: The work of system one through the displacements of system two equals the converse.
source: BEU syllabus — Structural Analysis, Unit 2

unit_title: Energy Methods: Principle of minimum potential energy Principle of virtual
stem: Maxwell's reciprocal theorem is the theoretical basis of:
options: The symmetry of flexibility and stiffness matrices
explanation: It also underlies the Muller Breslau principle.
source: BEU syllabus — Structural Analysis, Unit 2

unit_title: Energy Methods: Principle of minimum potential energy Principle of virtual
stem: A limitation of Castigliano's theorems is that they apply strictly to:
options: Linearly elastic structures obeying Hooke's law
explanation: The Crotti Engesser theorem extends them to non-linear elasticity.
source: BEU syllabus — Structural Analysis, Unit 2

unit_title: Energy Methods: Principle of minimum potential energy Principle of virtual
stem: The Crotti Engesser theorem uses:
options: Complementary strain energy differentiated with respect to load
Strain energy with respect to displacement
explanation: It is valid for non-linear elastic behaviour.
source: BEU syllabus — Structural Analysis, Unit 2

unit_title: Energy Methods: Principle of minimum potential energy Principle of virtual
stem: Applying the theorem of least work to a propped cantilever gives the prop reaction from:
options: Setting the derivative of strain energy with respect to the prop reaction to zero
explanation: The support does no work since its deflection is zero.
source: BEU syllabus — Structural Analysis, Unit 2

unit_title: Energy Methods: Principle of minimum potential energy Principle of virtual

stem: Strain energy per unit volume for a bar under uniaxial stress sigma is:

source: BEU syllabus — Structural Analysis, Unit 2

unit_title: Energy Methods: Principle of minimum potential energy Principle of virtual
stem: For a truss, the internal virtual work under a unit virtual load is:
explanation: Here delta L is the real elongation of each member.
source: BEU syllabus — Structural Analysis, Unit 2

unit_title: Energy Methods: Principle of minimum potential energy Principle of virtual
stem: Castigliano's second theorem can be applied to non-linear elastic structures directly.
explanation: It requires linear elasticity; the Crotti Engesser theorem covers the non-linear case.
source: BEU syllabus — Structural Analysis, Unit 2

unit_title: Energy Methods: Principle of minimum potential energy Principle of virtual
topic: Strain energy and principle of minimum potential energy
stem: For a linear elastic body, complementary strain energy equals strain energy.
explanation: The load deformation relationship is a straight line, dividing the rectangle equally.
source: BEU syllabus — Structural Analysis, Unit 2

unit_title: Energy Methods: Principle of minimum potential energy Principle of virtual
stem:
Assertion (A): The theorem of least work is useful for analysing indeterminate structures.
Reason (R): Redundant reactions correspond to points of zero displacement, so the strain energy derivative vanishes.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: This gives one equation per redundant.
source: BEU syllabus — Structural Analysis, Unit 2

unit_title: Energy Methods: Principle of minimum potential energy Principle of virtual
topic: Strain energy and principle of minimum potential energy
stem:
Assertion (A): The principle of minimum potential energy underlies the finite element method.
Reason (R): Assumed displacement fields are made to minimise total potential energy over the element mesh.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: This yields the element stiffness equations.
source: BEU syllabus — Structural Analysis, Unit 2

unit_title: Energy Methods: Principle of minimum potential energy Principle of virtual
stem: Which of the following are energy theorems used in structural analysis?
explanation: There is no Manning theorem in structural analysis.
source: BEU syllabus — Structural Analysis, Unit 2

unit_title: Muller Breslau Principles and its applications to determinate and indeterminate
topic: Muller Breslau principle: statement and basis
stem: The Muller Breslau principle states that the influence line for a function is given by:
options: The deflected shape obtained by removing the restraint corresponding to that function and imposing a unit displacement
explanation: The deflected shape is proportional to the influence line.
source: BEU syllabus — Structural Analysis, Unit 3

unit_title: Muller Breslau Principles and its applications to determinate and indeterminate
topic: Muller Breslau principle: statement and basis
stem: The Muller Breslau principle is based on:
explanation: It therefore requires linear elastic behaviour.
source: BEU syllabus — Structural Analysis, Unit 3

unit_title: Muller Breslau Principles and its applications to determinate and indeterminate
topic: Muller Breslau principle: statement and basis
stem: A fundamental limitation of the Muller Breslau principle is that it applies only to:
options: Linearly elastic structures with small displacements
explanation: Superposition must be valid for the principle to hold.
source: BEU syllabus — Structural Analysis, Unit 3

unit_title: Muller Breslau Principles and its applications to determinate and indeterminate
topic: Muller Breslau principle: statement and basis
stem: To draw the influence line for a support reaction using Muller Breslau, one:
options: Removes the support and gives a unit displacement in the direction of the reaction
explanation: The resulting deflected shape is the influence line.
source: BEU syllabus — Structural Analysis, Unit 3

unit_title: Muller Breslau Principles and its applications to determinate and indeterminate
topic: Muller Breslau principle: statement and basis
stem: To draw the influence line for bending moment at a section, one:
options: Inserts a hinge at the section and imposes a unit relative rotation
explanation: The relative rotation of the two faces is made unity.
source: BEU syllabus — Structural Analysis, Unit 3

unit_title: Muller Breslau Principles and its applications to determinate and indeterminate
topic: Muller Breslau principle: statement and basis
stem: To obtain the influence line for shear force at a section, one:
options: Introduces a shear release and imposes a unit relative transverse displacement
explanation: The two faces remain parallel but displace relative to each other.
source: BEU syllabus — Structural Analysis, Unit 3

unit_title: Muller Breslau Principles and its applications to determinate and indeterminate
topic: Muller Breslau principle: statement and basis
stem: The ordinate of an influence line drawn by the Muller Breslau principle must be:
options: Scaled so the imposed displacement or rotation equals unity
explanation: Otherwise only the qualitative shape is obtained.
source: BEU syllabus — Structural Analysis, Unit 3

unit_title: Muller Breslau Principles and its applications to determinate and indeterminate
topic: Muller Breslau principle: statement and basis
stem: Muller Breslau's principle is especially valuable because:
options: It allows qualitative influence lines to be sketched quickly for complex structures
explanation: Qualitative shapes reveal the critical load positions immediately.
source: BEU syllabus — Structural Analysis, Unit 3

unit_title: Muller Breslau Principles and its applications to determinate and indeterminate
stem: For a simply supported beam, the influence line for reaction at A obtained by Muller Breslau is:
options: A triangle with unit ordinate at A falling linearly to zero at B
A curve with zero at A
explanation: Determinate structures give straight line influence diagrams.
source: BEU syllabus — Structural Analysis, Unit 3

unit_title: Muller Breslau Principles and its applications to determinate and indeterminate
stem: The influence line for bending moment at midspan C of a simply supported beam of span L is:
options: A parabola with peak L by 8
A triangle with peak ordinate L by 4 at C
explanation: The two segments have slopes of one half.
source: BEU syllabus — Structural Analysis, Unit 3

unit_title: Muller Breslau Principles and its applications to determinate and indeterminate
stem: The influence line for shear at a section C of a simply supported beam consists of:
options: Two parallel straight lines with a unit jump at C
explanation: The ordinates just left and right of C are minus b/L and a/L.
source: BEU syllabus — Structural Analysis, Unit 3

unit_title: Muller Breslau Principles and its applications to determinate and indeterminate
stem: For a determinate structure, the deflected shape produced by the Muller Breslau release is:
options: A rigid body displacement composed of straight segments
explanation: The released determinate structure becomes a mechanism.
source: BEU syllabus — Structural Analysis, Unit 3

unit_title: Muller Breslau Principles and its applications to determinate and indeterminate
stem: For an overhanging beam, the influence line for reaction at the interior support extends:
options: Beyond the support with negative ordinates over the overhang
explanation: Loads on the overhang can reduce that reaction.
source: BEU syllabus — Structural Analysis, Unit 3

unit_title: Muller Breslau Principles and its applications to determinate and indeterminate
stem: The influence line for the force in a truss member can be obtained by:
options: Removing that member and imposing a unit relative axial displacement
Inserting a hinge at a joint
explanation: The resulting joint displacements form the influence line.
source: BEU syllabus — Structural Analysis, Unit 3

unit_title: Muller Breslau Principles and its applications to determinate and indeterminate
stem: The area under a bending moment influence line multiplied by a uniformly distributed load intensity gives:
options: The bending moment at that section due to the distributed load
explanation: Only the loaded length of the influence line is integrated.
source: BEU syllabus — Structural Analysis, Unit 3

unit_title: Muller Breslau Principles and its applications to determinate and indeterminate
stem: Using influence lines, the maximum positive shear at a section under a moving uniformly distributed load requires:

explanation: Loading the negative region would reduce the response.
source: BEU syllabus — Structural Analysis, Unit 3

unit_title: Muller Breslau Principles and its applications to determinate and indeterminate
stem: Influence lines for indeterminate structures obtained by Muller Breslau's principle are:
options: Curved because the released structure remains elastic and continuous
explanation: The remaining redundancy keeps the structure elastic under the imposed displacement.
source: BEU syllabus — Structural Analysis, Unit 3

unit_title: Muller Breslau Principles and its applications to determinate and indeterminate
stem: For a two span continuous beam, the influence line for the central support reaction is drawn by:

explanation: The resulting elastic curve is the influence line.
source: BEU syllabus — Structural Analysis, Unit 3

unit_title: Muller Breslau Principles and its applications to determinate and indeterminate
stem: For indeterminate structures, quantitative influence line ordinates require:
options: Computing the elastic deflected shape of the released structure
explanation: Methods such as the flexibility approach are used.
source: BEU syllabus — Structural Analysis, Unit 3

unit_title: Muller Breslau Principles and its applications to determinate and indeterminate
stem: For a continuous beam, the maximum positive bending moment at midspan of a span occurs when live load covers:
explanation: Chequerboard or alternate span loading follows from the influence line.
source: BEU syllabus — Structural Analysis, Unit 3

unit_title: Muller Breslau Principles and its applications to determinate and indeterminate
stem: The maximum hogging moment over an interior support of a continuous beam occurs when live load covers:

explanation: The influence line is negative over these spans.
source: BEU syllabus — Structural Analysis, Unit 3

unit_title: Muller Breslau Principles and its applications to determinate and indeterminate
stem: Pattern loading in continuous beam design is determined from:

source: BEU syllabus — Structural Analysis, Unit 3

unit_title: Muller Breslau Principles and its applications to determinate and indeterminate
stem: A qualitative influence line sketch for an indeterminate frame is useful for:
options: Deciding the pattern of live load producing the critical response
explanation: Exact analysis follows once the pattern is fixed.
source: BEU syllabus — Structural Analysis, Unit 3

unit_title: Muller Breslau Principles and its applications to determinate and indeterminate
stem: For a propped cantilever, the influence line for the propping reaction is obtained by:

Removing the prop and imposing a unit displacement at that point on the remaining cantilever
Inserting a hinge at the fixed end
explanation: The elastic curve of the cantilever gives the ordinates.
source: BEU syllabus — Structural Analysis, Unit 3

unit_title: Muller Breslau Principles and its applications to determinate and indeterminate

Releasing the rotational restraint and imposing a unit rotation there

source: BEU syllabus — Structural Analysis, Unit 3

unit_title: Muller Breslau Principles and its applications to determinate and indeterminate
stem: Muller Breslau's principle applied to indeterminate structures is sometimes called:

unit_title: Muller Breslau Principles and its applications to determinate and indeterminate
topic: Muller Breslau principle: statement and basis
stem: If the imposed displacement in the Muller Breslau procedure is not unity, the deflected shape:
options: Must be divided by the imposed displacement to give the influence line
explanation: Scaling preserves the correct ordinates.
source: BEU syllabus — Structural Analysis, Unit 3

unit_title: Muller Breslau Principles and its applications to determinate and indeterminate
stem: The influence line for the bending moment at the fixed end of a cantilever of length L is:

unit_title: Muller Breslau Principles and its applications to determinate and indeterminate
topic: Muller Breslau principle: statement and basis
stem: Muller Breslau's principle was established in the year:

unit_title: Muller Breslau Principles and its applications to determinate and indeterminate

unit_title: Muller Breslau Principles and its applications to determinate and indeterminate

stem: Muller Breslau's principle is valid for structures loaded beyond the elastic limit.

unit_title: Muller Breslau Principles and its applications to determinate and indeterminate
stem:

Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

source: BEU syllabus — Structural Analysis, Unit 3

unit_title: Muller Breslau Principles and its applications to determinate and indeterminate

stem: Muller Breslau's principle can be used to obtain influence lines for:

A is false but R is true

topic: Scope of geology in civil engineering
stem:
Assertion (A): Site investigation must include geological mapping for major projects.

Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A

A is false but R is true

stem: A ductile material is characterised by:

Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A

A is false but R is true

Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A

A is false but R is true

Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A

Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A

A is false but R is true

Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A

A is false but R is true

stem:
Assertion (A): Centrifugal pumps must be primed before starting.

options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Self priming designs incorporate a small liquid reservoir.
source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering [101504], Unit 1

stem: Energy thickness is defined by the integral of:

stem: Shape factor of a boundary layer is the ratio of:

source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering [101504], Unit 2

topic: Laminar and turbulent boundary layers on a flat plate
stem: On a flat plate, the boundary layer is normally laminar up to a Reynolds number of about:

stem: According to Blasius, the laminar boundary layer thickness on a flat plate varies as:

source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering [101504], Unit 2

Suction of the low energy fluid through slots

stem:
Assertion (A): Dimples on a golf ball reduce the total drag.

Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering [101504], Unit 2

stem:

options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

source: BEU syllabus — Hydraulic Engineering [101504], Unit 2

Flow parameters at a section do not change with time

A is false but R is true
