topic: Flexural and torsional buckling of compression members
stem: Torsional flexural buckling is significant for:
options: Singly symmetric and unsymmetric open thin walled sections
explanation: Angles and channels are susceptible.
source: BEU syllabus — Design of Steel Structure, Unit 4

unit_title: Design For Flexural And Flexural-torsional Buckling
topic: Flexural and torsional buckling of compression members
stem: The maximum permissible slenderness ratio for a compression member carrying loads from dead and imposed loads is:
explanation: For bracing resisting wind only it may be 250.
source: BEU syllabus — Design of Steel Structure, Unit 4

unit_title: Design For Flexural And Flexural-torsional Buckling
topic: Flexural and torsional buckling of compression members
stem: A laced column has lacing bars designed for a transverse shear of:
options: 2.5 percent of the axial force in the column
explanation: Lacing must also satisfy its own slenderness limit.
source: BEU syllabus — Design of Steel Structure, Unit 4

unit_title: Design For Flexural And Flexural-torsional Buckling
topic: Flexural and torsional buckling of compression members
stem: Battened columns are less efficient than laced columns because:
options: Battens resist shear by bending, giving lower shear stiffness
explanation: The slenderness of a battened column is increased by 10 percent.
source: BEU syllabus — Design of Steel Structure, Unit 4

unit_title: Design For Flexural And Flexural-torsional Buckling
topic: Flexural and torsional buckling of compression members
stem: A slab base of a column transmits load to the concrete by:
options: Direct bearing over the base plate area
explanation: The plate thickness is designed for the bearing pressure cantilever moment.
source: BEU syllabus — Design of Steel Structure, Unit 4

unit_title: Design For Flexural And Flexural-torsional Buckling
stem: Lateral torsional buckling reduces the moment capacity of an unrestrained beam.
explanation: The beam fails by combined lateral deflection and twist before reaching the plastic moment.
source: BEU syllabus — Design of Steel Structure, Unit 4

unit_title: Design For Flexural And Flexural-torsional Buckling
topic: Flexural and torsional buckling of compression members
stem: A column always buckles about the axis with the largest radius of gyration.
explanation: Buckling occurs about the axis giving the highest slenderness, generally the least radius of gyration.
source: BEU syllabus — Design of Steel Structure, Unit 4

unit_title: Design For Flexural And Flexural-torsional Buckling
stem:
Assertion (A): Closed hollow sections rarely fail by lateral torsional buckling.
Reason (R): Their very high torsional rigidity resists the twisting component of the buckling mode.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Open thin walled sections have low torsional stiffness.
source: BEU syllabus — Design of Steel Structure, Unit 4

unit_title: Design For Flexural And Flexural-torsional Buckling
topic: Flexural behaviour of beams and laterally restrained design
stem:
Assertion (A): Bearing stiffeners are provided under concentrated loads on plate girders.
Reason (R): They prevent web crippling and web buckling by transferring load directly to the flanges.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: They are designed as struts with an effective web width.
source: BEU syllabus — Design of Steel Structure, Unit 4

unit_title: Design For Flexural And Flexural-torsional Buckling
topic: Flexural and torsional buckling of compression members
stem: Which factors influence the compressive strength of a steel column?
explanation: Concrete properties are irrelevant for a bare steel column.
source: BEU syllabus — Design of Steel Structure, Unit 4

topic: Shear strength of webs and shear buckling
stem: In an I section beam, shear is assumed to be resisted mainly by:
explanation: Flanges resist most of the bending moment.
source: BEU syllabus — Design of Steel Structure, Unit 5

topic: Shear strength of webs and shear buckling
stem: The plastic shear resistance of a section is based on:
options: The von Mises shear yield stress of fy over root three
explanation: It is applied over the shear area of the web.
source: BEU syllabus — Design of Steel Structure, Unit 5

topic: Shear strength of webs and shear buckling
stem: The shear area of a rolled I section loaded parallel to the web is taken as:
explanation: For welded sections it is the clear web depth times thickness.
source: BEU syllabus — Design of Steel Structure, Unit 5

topic: Shear strength of webs and shear buckling
stem: A web is susceptible to shear buckling when:
options: The depth to thickness ratio exceeds about 67 epsilon for unstiffened webs
explanation: Slender webs require intermediate transverse stiffeners.
source: BEU syllabus — Design of Steel Structure, Unit 5

topic: Shear strength of webs and shear buckling
stem: The simple post critical method of computing shear buckling strength:
options: Ignores any post buckling tension field contribution
explanation: The tension field method gives higher strength but needs proper anchorage.
source: BEU syllabus — Design of Steel Structure, Unit 5

topic: Shear strength of webs and shear buckling
stem: The elastic critical shear stress of a web panel depends on:
options: The panel aspect ratio and the depth to thickness ratio
explanation: Closer stiffener spacing raises the buckling coefficient.
source: BEU syllabus — Design of Steel Structure, Unit 5

topic: Shear strength of webs and shear buckling
stem: Shear stress distribution across an I section web is:
options: Approximately parabolic with the maximum at the neutral axis
explanation: The average value is often used for design simplicity.
source: BEU syllabus — Design of Steel Structure, Unit 5

topic: Shear strength of webs and shear buckling
stem: A web panel in tension field action behaves like:
options: A Pratt truss with the web forming diagonal tension ties
explanation: Stiffeners act as vertical compression struts.
source: BEU syllabus — Design of Steel Structure, Unit 5

topic: Shear strength of webs and shear buckling
stem: Shear buckling of a web is best prevented economically by:
options: Providing intermediate transverse stiffeners rather than thickening the web
explanation: Stiffeners reduce the effective panel dimensions.
source: BEU syllabus — Design of Steel Structure, Unit 5

stem: Shear moment interaction must be considered when the design shear exceeds:
explanation: Below this value the full moment capacity may be used.
source: BEU syllabus — Design of Steel Structure, Unit 5

stem: In the reduced moment capacity expression, the factor beta is:
explanation: It is zero when V equals half of Vd.
source: BEU syllabus — Design of Steel Structure, Unit 5

stem: The reduced plastic moment capacity in the presence of high shear is:
explanation: Mfd is the plastic moment capacity of the flanges alone.
source: BEU syllabus — Design of Steel Structure, Unit 5

stem: Mfd in the shear moment interaction equation represents:
options: Plastic moment capacity of the flanges only, after deducting the web
explanation: The web is assumed fully used for shear.
source: BEU syllabus — Design of Steel Structure, Unit 5

stem: High shear combined with high moment is most likely at:
options: Mid span of a simply supported beam
The interior support of a continuous beam
explanation: Both shear and hogging moment peak there.
source: BEU syllabus — Design of Steel Structure, Unit 5

stem: The physical basis of shear moment interaction is that:
options: The web cannot simultaneously develop its full shear and full bending stress
explanation: Von Mises yielding under combined stress governs.
source: BEU syllabus — Design of Steel Structure, Unit 5

stem: For a section with slender web the interaction check uses:
options: The shear buckling strength in place of the plastic shear capacity
explanation: Buckling rather than yield governs the web.
source: BEU syllabus — Design of Steel Structure, Unit 5

stem: Combined bending, shear and axial force in a member is checked using:
options: An interaction equation given in IS 800 section 9
explanation: Both section strength and overall member strength are verified.
source: BEU syllabus — Design of Steel Structure, Unit 5

stem: For low shear beams, the design moment capacity is:
explanation: No reduction is required below 0.6Vd.
source: BEU syllabus — Design of Steel Structure, Unit 5

topic: Stiffeners, plate girders and design checks
stem: A plate girder is used when:
options: Loads and spans are too large for available rolled sections
explanation: It is fabricated from plates welded together.
source: BEU syllabus — Design of Steel Structure, Unit 5

topic: Stiffeners, plate girders and design checks
stem: Bearing stiffeners in a plate girder are provided:
options: At supports and under concentrated loads
explanation: They are designed as struts with a portion of the web.
source: BEU syllabus — Design of Steel Structure, Unit 5

topic: Stiffeners, plate girders and design checks
stem: Intermediate transverse stiffeners primarily:
options: Increase the shear buckling strength of the web panels
explanation: They divide the web into smaller panels.
source: BEU syllabus — Design of Steel Structure, Unit 5

topic: Stiffeners, plate girders and design checks
stem: A longitudinal stiffener in a deep girder web is provided to:
options: Improve resistance to bending induced buckling of the web
explanation: It is placed in the compression zone of the web.
source: BEU syllabus — Design of Steel Structure, Unit 5

topic: Stiffeners, plate girders and design checks
stem: The web to flange weld in a plate girder is designed for:
options: The horizontal shear flow between web and flange
explanation: Shear flow equals VQ over I.
source: BEU syllabus — Design of Steel Structure, Unit 5

topic: Stiffeners, plate girders and design checks
stem: Curtailment of flange plates in a plate girder is done to:
options: Economise material where the bending moment is smaller
explanation: The theoretical cut off point is extended for development length.
source: BEU syllabus — Design of Steel Structure, Unit 5

topic: Stiffeners, plate girders and design checks
stem: The optimum economical depth of a plate girder is one that:
options: Minimises the total weight of the flanges and web
explanation: Practical depth is often span over 10 to span over 12.
source: BEU syllabus — Design of Steel Structure, Unit 5

topic: Stiffeners, plate girders and design checks
stem: A splice in a plate girder flange should preferably be:
options: A full penetration butt weld located away from the maximum moment
explanation: Web and flange splices are staggered.
source: BEU syllabus — Design of Steel Structure, Unit 5

topic: Stiffeners, plate girders and design checks
stem: End post design in a girder using tension field action is important because:
options: It must anchor the horizontal component of the tension field
explanation: A double stiffener end post is often required.
source: BEU syllabus — Design of Steel Structure, Unit 5

topic: Stiffeners, plate girders and design checks
stem: A gantry girder is subject to:
options: Vertical, lateral surge and longitudinal braking forces
explanation: Fatigue is also a key design consideration.
source: BEU syllabus — Design of Steel Structure, Unit 5

stem: Shear moment interaction need not be checked when the shear is below 0.6 times the design shear strength.
explanation: Below this level the web can still develop its full contribution to bending.
source: BEU syllabus — Design of Steel Structure, Unit 5

topic: Stiffeners, plate girders and design checks
stem: Intermediate stiffeners in a plate girder mainly increase the bending strength.
explanation: They mainly increase the shear buckling resistance of the web panels.
source: BEU syllabus — Design of Steel Structure, Unit 5

topic: Shear strength of webs and shear buckling
stem:
Assertion (A): Tension field action allows a web panel to carry shear beyond elastic buckling.
Reason (R): After buckling the web develops diagonal tension anchored by the flanges and stiffeners.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Adequate end posts are essential for this mechanism.
source: BEU syllabus — Design of Steel Structure, Unit 5

stem:
Assertion (A): The flanges alone provide the residual moment capacity under very high shear.
Reason (R): The web is assumed to be fully utilised in resisting shear and unavailable for bending.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: This is the basis of the Mfd term in the interaction formula.
source: BEU syllabus — Design of Steel Structure, Unit 5

topic: Stiffeners, plate girders and design checks
stem: Which stiffeners may be used in a plate girder?
options: Longitudinal stiffeners in the compression zone
Tension stiffeners in the flange plate
explanation: There is no recognised category called tension stiffener in the flange.
source: BEU syllabus — Design of Steel Structure, Unit 5

topic: Behaviour of beam columns under combined loading
stem: A beam column is a member subjected to:
options: Combined axial compression and bending moment
explanation: Columns of rigid frames are typical beam columns.
source: BEU syllabus — Design of Steel Structure, Unit 6

topic: Behaviour of beam columns under combined loading
stem: The P delta effect in a beam column refers to:
options: Additional moment produced by the axial force acting on the deflected shape
explanation: It is a second order geometric nonlinearity.
source: BEU syllabus — Design of Steel Structure, Unit 6

topic: Behaviour of beam columns under combined loading
stem: The P small delta effect is associated with:
explanation: P capital delta relates to storey sway.
source: BEU syllabus — Design of Steel Structure, Unit 6

topic: Behaviour of beam columns under combined loading
stem: The moment amplification factor for a beam column in a non sway frame is:
explanation: Cm depends on the shape of the moment diagram.
source: BEU syllabus — Design of Steel Structure, Unit 6

topic: Behaviour of beam columns under combined loading
stem: The equivalent uniform moment factor Cm is smallest when:
options: It is in single curvature with equal end moments
The member is bent in double curvature
explanation: Double curvature is less severe for stability.
source: BEU syllabus — Design of Steel Structure, Unit 6

topic: Behaviour of beam columns under combined loading
stem: A sway frame is one in which:
options: Lateral displacement of the storeys is not prevented by bracing or shear walls
explanation: Effective length factors exceed unity for such columns.
source: BEU syllabus — Design of Steel Structure, Unit 6

topic: Behaviour of beam columns under combined loading
stem: Bracing a frame converts it to a non sway frame, which:
options: Reduces the effective length of the columns
explanation: Effective length factor becomes less than or equal to 1.
source: BEU syllabus — Design of Steel Structure, Unit 6

topic: Behaviour of beam columns under combined loading
stem: A frame may be classified as non sway if the elastic buckling load factor is:
explanation: Second order effects are then small enough to be ignored.
source: BEU syllabus — Design of Steel Structure, Unit 6

topic: Behaviour of beam columns under combined loading
stem: Notional horizontal loads are applied in frame analysis to account for:
options: Initial out of plumb and other geometric imperfections
explanation: They are typically 0.5 percent of the factored gravity load.
source: BEU syllabus — Design of Steel Structure, Unit 6

stem: The section strength check for a beam column combines:
options: Axial force and bending moments about both axes
explanation: An interaction expression with exponents depending on the section is used.
source: BEU syllabus — Design of Steel Structure, Unit 6

stem: The simplest conservative interaction equation for a beam column is:
explanation: More refined expressions use exponents greater than one.
source: BEU syllabus — Design of Steel Structure, Unit 6

stem: The overall member strength check for a beam column must include:
options: Buckling resistance about both axes and lateral torsional buckling
explanation: Both in plane and out of plane behaviour must be verified.
source: BEU syllabus — Design of Steel Structure, Unit 6

stem: In the overall buckling check, the axial term uses:
options: The design compressive strength based on the relevant slenderness
explanation: The smaller of the strengths about the two axes governs.
source: BEU syllabus — Design of Steel Structure, Unit 6

stem: The Ky and Kz factors in the IS 800 beam column interaction equations are:
options: Moment amplification factors accounting for second order effects
explanation: They depend on the non dimensional slenderness and Cm.
source: BEU syllabus — Design of Steel Structure, Unit 6

stem: KLT in the interaction equation relates to:
options: Lateral torsional buckling under the major axis moment
explanation: It is used with the design bending strength Mdz.
source: BEU syllabus — Design of Steel Structure, Unit 6

stem: For a member under axial tension and bending, the check is:
options: An interaction of the reduced effective moment with tension capacity
explanation: Tension tends to stabilise, so buckling is not a concern.
source: BEU syllabus — Design of Steel Structure, Unit 6

stem: Biaxial bending with axial compression is most severe for:
options: Corner columns of a building frame
explanation: They receive unbalanced moments from two directions.
source: BEU syllabus — Design of Steel Structure, Unit 6

stem: A column in a sway frame designed with an effective length factor less than one would be:
options: Unsafe, since sway increases the effective length
explanation: Sway columns have K greater than one.
source: BEU syllabus — Design of Steel Structure, Unit 6

topic: Column bases, frames and practical detailing
stem: A slab base is generally used when the column carries:
options: Axial load with little or no moment
explanation: A gusseted base is used for larger loads and moments.
source: BEU syllabus — Design of Steel Structure, Unit 6

topic: Column bases, frames and practical detailing
stem: The thickness of a slab base plate is determined by:
options: The cantilever bending moment due to the uniform bearing pressure
explanation: A minimum thickness equal to the flange thickness is also required.
source: BEU syllabus — Design of Steel Structure, Unit 6

topic: Column bases, frames and practical detailing
stem: Anchor bolts in a moment resisting column base:
options: Resist the uplift tension on one side of the base
explanation: A shear key may be provided to resist horizontal force.
source: BEU syllabus — Design of Steel Structure, Unit 6

topic: Column bases, frames and practical detailing
stem: Grouting under a column base plate is provided to:
options: Ensure uniform bearing on the concrete pedestal
explanation: Non shrink grout is used after levelling the plate.
source: BEU syllabus — Design of Steel Structure, Unit 6

topic: Column bases, frames and practical detailing
stem: The permissible bearing strength of concrete under a base plate is taken as:
explanation: Confinement by the surrounding concrete allows this value.
source: BEU syllabus — Design of Steel Structure, Unit 6

topic: Column bases, frames and practical detailing
stem: A portal frame knee joint must be designed to:
options: Transfer the full moment with adequate stiffness, often using haunches
explanation: Diagonal stiffeners in the panel zone are often required.
source: BEU syllabus — Design of Steel Structure, Unit 6

topic: Column bases, frames and practical detailing
stem: Purlins in an industrial building are designed as:
options: Beams subject to biaxial bending due to the sloping roof
explanation: Channel and cold formed Z sections are commonly used.
source: BEU syllabus — Design of Steel Structure, Unit 6

topic: Column bases, frames and practical detailing
stem: Sag rods in a purlin system are provided to:
options: Reduce bending about the weak axis of the purlin
explanation: They act as intermediate supports in the plane of the roof.
source: BEU syllabus — Design of Steel Structure, Unit 6

topic: Column bases, frames and practical detailing
stem: Plastic design of a portal frame determines the collapse load by:
options: Identifying the mechanism with the lowest load factor
explanation: Beam, sway and combined mechanisms are examined.
source: BEU syllabus — Design of Steel Structure, Unit 6

topic: Column bases, frames and practical detailing
stem: A haunch at the eaves of a portal frame is provided to:
options: Increase the moment capacity where the moment is largest
explanation: It also improves the bolted connection lever arm.
source: BEU syllabus — Design of Steel Structure, Unit 6

topic: Behaviour of beam columns under combined loading
stem: The P delta effect increases the moments in a slender beam column.
explanation: Axial force acting on the deflected geometry produces additional second order moment.
source: BEU syllabus — Design of Steel Structure, Unit 6

topic: Column bases, frames and practical detailing
stem: A slab base is suitable where large moments must be transferred to the foundation.
explanation: Gusseted or moment resisting bases with anchor bolts are required for large moments.
source: BEU syllabus — Design of Steel Structure, Unit 6

topic: Behaviour of beam columns under combined loading
stem:
Assertion (A): Bracing a multistorey frame reduces the effective length of its columns.
Reason (R): Preventing sway restricts the buckling mode to one with a shorter half wavelength.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Sway frames have effective length factors greater than unity.
source: BEU syllabus — Design of Steel Structure, Unit 6

stem:
Assertion (A): Corner columns generally require a biaxial bending check.
Reason (R): They receive unbalanced beam moments about both principal axes simultaneously.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Interior columns tend to have more balanced moments.
source: BEU syllabus — Design of Steel Structure, Unit 6

stem: Which checks are required for a beam column in IS 800:2007?
options: Overall member buckling about both axes
explanation: Shrinkage is a concrete phenomenon, not applicable to steel members.
source: BEU syllabus — Design of Steel Structure, Unit 6

stem: Economics is best defined as the study of:
options: Allocation of scarce resources among competing uses
explanation: Scarcity and choice are its central problems.
source: BEU syllabus — Engineering Economics, Estimation & Costing, Unit 1

stem: The law of demand states that, other things remaining equal:
options: Quantity demanded falls as price rises
Quantity demanded rises as price rises
explanation: The demand curve therefore slopes downward.
source: BEU syllabus — Engineering Economics, Estimation & Costing, Unit 1

stem: Price elasticity of demand measures:
options: Percentage change in quantity demanded per percentage change in price
explanation: Demand is elastic when the value exceeds one.
source: BEU syllabus — Engineering Economics, Estimation & Costing, Unit 1

stem: Opportunity cost of a decision is:
options: The value of the next best alternative foregone
explanation: It is central to rational economic choice.
source: BEU syllabus — Engineering Economics, Estimation & Costing, Unit 1

stem: A sunk cost should be:
options: Ignored in future decision making since it cannot be recovered
explanation: Only future cash flows are relevant to decisions.
source: BEU syllabus — Engineering Economics, Estimation & Costing, Unit 1

stem: The law of diminishing marginal utility states that:
options: Additional satisfaction from each extra unit consumed declines
explanation: It explains the downward sloping demand curve.
source: BEU syllabus — Engineering Economics, Estimation & Costing, Unit 1

stem: In a perfectly competitive market:
options: Many buyers and sellers trade a homogeneous product and are price takers
explanation: Monopoly is the opposite extreme.
source: BEU syllabus — Engineering Economics, Estimation & Costing, Unit 1

stem: The break even point in production is where:
options: Total revenue equals total cost and profit is zero
explanation: It equals fixed cost divided by contribution per unit.
source: BEU syllabus — Engineering Economics, Estimation & Costing, Unit 1

stem: The law of supply implies that the supply curve:
options: Slopes upward as higher prices induce more production
explanation: Equilibrium occurs where supply meets demand.
source: BEU syllabus — Engineering Economics, Estimation & Costing, Unit 1

topic: Time value of money and project evaluation
stem: The time value of money implies that:
options: A rupee today is worth more than a rupee in the future
explanation: Money can earn interest over time.
source: BEU syllabus — Engineering Economics, Estimation & Costing, Unit 1

topic: Time value of money and project evaluation
stem: The compound amount factor for a single payment is:
explanation: Its reciprocal is the present worth factor.
source: BEU syllabus — Engineering Economics, Estimation & Costing, Unit 1

topic: Time value of money and project evaluation
stem: The capital recovery factor converts:
options: A present sum into an equivalent uniform annual series
An annual series into a future sum
explanation: It is used to compute equated annual instalments.
source: BEU syllabus — Engineering Economics, Estimation & Costing, Unit 1

topic: Time value of money and project evaluation
stem: Net present value of a project is:
options: The sum of discounted cash inflows minus discounted outflows
explanation: A positive NPV indicates an economically acceptable project.
source: BEU syllabus — Engineering Economics, Estimation & Costing, Unit 1

topic: Time value of money and project evaluation
stem: The internal rate of return is the discount rate at which:
options: The net present value of a project becomes zero
explanation: A project is accepted if the IRR exceeds the cost of capital.
source: BEU syllabus — Engineering Economics, Estimation & Costing, Unit 1

topic: Time value of money and project evaluation
stem: The benefit cost ratio method accepts a project if the ratio is:
explanation: It is widely used in public sector project appraisal.
source: BEU syllabus — Engineering Economics, Estimation & Costing, Unit 1

topic: Time value of money and project evaluation
stem: The payback period method is criticised because it:
options: Ignores cash flows after the payback and the time value of money
explanation: It is still popular as a simple risk indicator.
source: BEU syllabus — Engineering Economics, Estimation & Costing, Unit 1

topic: Time value of money and project evaluation
stem: For mutually exclusive alternatives of unequal life, comparison should be based on:
options: Equivalent uniform annual cost over a common study period
explanation: Alternatively a least common multiple of lives is used.
source: BEU syllabus — Engineering Economics, Estimation & Costing, Unit 1

topic: Time value of money and project evaluation
stem: Inflation affects project evaluation because:
options: Nominal and real cash flows must be discounted consistently
explanation: Real flows use the real discount rate.
source: BEU syllabus — Engineering Economics, Estimation & Costing, Unit 1

topic: Cost concepts, depreciation and decision making
stem: Fixed cost is a cost that:
options: Does not vary with the level of output in the short run
explanation: Rent and salaries are examples.
source: BEU syllabus — Engineering Economics, Estimation & Costing, Unit 1

topic: Cost concepts, depreciation and decision making
stem: Marginal cost is:
options: The additional cost of producing one more unit
explanation: Profit is maximised where marginal cost equals marginal revenue.
source: BEU syllabus — Engineering Economics, Estimation & Costing, Unit 1

topic: Cost concepts, depreciation and decision making
stem: Depreciation of an asset represents:
options: The loss of value due to use, wear and obsolescence
explanation: It is charged against income over the useful life.
source: BEU syllabus — Engineering Economics, Estimation & Costing, Unit 1

topic: Cost concepts, depreciation and decision making
stem: In the straight line method, annual depreciation equals:
options: Cost minus salvage value, divided by useful life
A fixed percentage of book value
explanation: It gives a uniform charge every year.
source: BEU syllabus — Engineering Economics, Estimation & Costing, Unit 1

topic: Cost concepts, depreciation and decision making
stem: The declining balance method of depreciation:
options: Applies a fixed rate to the reducing book value each year
explanation: It front loads the depreciation charge.
source: BEU syllabus — Engineering Economics, Estimation & Costing, Unit 1

topic: Cost concepts, depreciation and decision making
stem: The sinking fund method of depreciation assumes:
options: Periodic deposits earning interest accumulate to the replacement cost
explanation: Early year charges are lower than in the straight line method.
source: BEU syllabus — Engineering Economics, Estimation & Costing, Unit 1

topic: Cost concepts, depreciation and decision making
stem: Obsolescence differs from physical deterioration because it is caused by:
options: Technological change making the asset outdated
explanation: An asset may be obsolete while still physically sound.
source: BEU syllabus — Engineering Economics, Estimation & Costing, Unit 1

topic: Cost concepts, depreciation and decision making
stem: A make or buy decision should be based on:
options: Comparison of relevant incremental costs of the two options
explanation: Quality, capacity and strategic factors also matter.
source: BEU syllabus — Engineering Economics, Estimation & Costing, Unit 1

topic: Cost concepts, depreciation and decision making
stem: A replacement analysis compares the defender with the challenger, where the defender is:
explanation: Replacement is justified when the challenger's EUAC is lower.
source: BEU syllabus — Engineering Economics, Estimation & Costing, Unit 1

topic: Cost concepts, depreciation and decision making
stem: Sensitivity analysis in project evaluation examines:
options: How the outcome changes when key input assumptions vary
explanation: It identifies the most critical variables.
source: BEU syllabus — Engineering Economics, Estimation & Costing, Unit 1

topic: Time value of money and project evaluation
stem: A project with a positive net present value is economically acceptable.
explanation: It earns more than the required rate of return.
source: BEU syllabus — Engineering Economics, Estimation & Costing, Unit 1

stem: Sunk costs should be considered when deciding whether to continue a project.
explanation: Sunk costs are unrecoverable and irrelevant to future decisions.
source: BEU syllabus — Engineering Economics, Estimation & Costing, Unit 1

topic: Time value of money and project evaluation
stem:
Assertion (A): The payback period is a poor criterion for long lived infrastructure projects.
Reason (R): It ignores both the time value of money and all cash flows occurring after payback.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Discounted measures such as NPV or IRR are preferred.
source: BEU syllabus — Engineering Economics, Estimation & Costing, Unit 1

topic: Cost concepts, depreciation and decision making

stem: The inside clearance of a sampler is provided to:

explanation: It is usually 0.5 to 3 percent.
source: BEU syllabus — Geotechnical Engineering-II, Unit 3

stem: A split spoon sampler collects:
options: Disturbed but representative samples during the standard penetration test
explanation: Its area ratio is far above the undisturbed limit.
source: BEU syllabus — Geotechnical Engineering-II, Unit 3

stem: A piston sampler is preferred in very soft clays because it:
options: Prevents entry of excess soil and loss of sample during withdrawal
explanation: It gives the highest quality undisturbed samples.
source: BEU syllabus — Geotechnical Engineering-II, Unit 3

stem: Samples for laboratory testing must be:
options: Sealed with wax and transported carefully to preserve moisture and structure
explanation: Labelling with depth and borehole number is essential.
source: BEU syllabus — Geotechnical Engineering-II, Unit 3

stem: Rock quality designation is computed as the percentage of core recovered in pieces:
options: Longer than 100 mm, divided by the run length
explanation: RQD above 90 percent indicates excellent rock quality.
source: BEU syllabus — Geotechnical Engineering-II, Unit 3

stem: Core recovery in rock drilling is expressed as:
options: The length of core recovered divided by the length drilled
explanation: Low recovery may indicate weak or fractured rock.
source: BEU syllabus — Geotechnical Engineering-II, Unit 3

stem: The standard penetration test measures:
options: The number of blows to drive a split spoon sampler 300 mm
explanation: A 63.5 kg hammer falling through 750 mm is used.
source: BEU syllabus — Geotechnical Engineering-II, Unit 3

stem: Corrections applied to the observed SPT N value include:
explanation: Energy ratio correction to N60 is also applied.
source: BEU syllabus — Geotechnical Engineering-II, Unit 3

stem: The dilatancy correction to the SPT N value is applied for:
options: Fine saturated silts and sands with N greater than 15
explanation: It accounts for negative pore pressures during driving.
source: BEU syllabus — Geotechnical Engineering-II, Unit 3

stem: The static cone penetration test provides:
options: A continuous profile of cone resistance and sleeve friction
explanation: The friction ratio helps identify the soil type.
source: BEU syllabus — Geotechnical Engineering-II, Unit 3

stem: The vane shear test is used to determine:
options: The undrained shear strength of soft sensitive clays in situ
explanation: Sensitivity is obtained from the remoulded vane strength.
source: BEU syllabus — Geotechnical Engineering-II, Unit 3

stem: A plate load test is used to estimate:
options: Bearing capacity and settlement of shallow foundations
explanation: Scale effects must be considered when extrapolating to a full size footing.
source: BEU syllabus — Geotechnical Engineering-II, Unit 3

stem: The plate load test is unreliable in clays for settlement prediction because:
options: The stressed zone of a large footing is much deeper than that of the plate
explanation: Consolidation settlement is not captured in the short test.
source: BEU syllabus — Geotechnical Engineering-II, Unit 3

stem: The pressuremeter test measures:
options: In situ stress strain response of the ground from borehole expansion
explanation: It gives a pressuremeter modulus and limit pressure.
source: BEU syllabus — Geotechnical Engineering-II, Unit 3

stem: Seismic refraction surveying determines the subsurface profile from:
options: Travel times of refracted elastic waves through layers of different velocity
explanation: It requires velocity to increase with depth.
source: BEU syllabus — Geotechnical Engineering-II, Unit 3

stem: Electrical resistivity surveying is useful for:
options: Locating the water table, bedrock and contaminant plumes
explanation: The Wenner configuration is commonly used.
source: BEU syllabus — Geotechnical Engineering-II, Unit 3

stem: The area ratio of an undisturbed sampler should preferably be less than 10 percent.
explanation: A low area ratio minimises displacement and disturbance of the soil.
source: BEU syllabus — Geotechnical Engineering-II, Unit 3

stem: The split spoon sampler yields undisturbed samples.
explanation: It is a thick walled sampler giving disturbed but representative samples.
source: BEU syllabus — Geotechnical Engineering-II, Unit 3

stem:
Assertion (A): Geophysical methods are used to supplement rather than replace boring.
Reason (R): They give indirect and non unique interpretations that must be calibrated against borehole data.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: They cover large areas rapidly and economically.
source: BEU syllabus — Geotechnical Engineering-II, Unit 3

topic: Purpose, planning and extent of soil exploration
stem:
Assertion (A): Site investigation is a cost effective part of any project.
Reason (R): Its cost is a tiny fraction of project cost but it prevents far larger failure and overrun costs.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Most foundation problems trace back to inadequate investigation.
source: BEU syllabus — Geotechnical Engineering-II, Unit 3

stem: Which are in situ field tests used in geotechnical investigation?
explanation: Atterberg limits are determined in the laboratory.
source: BEU syllabus — Geotechnical Engineering-II, Unit 3

stem: Auger boring is best suited for:
options: Shallow depths in cohesive soils above the water table
Below the water table in sand
explanation: Hand augers are used to about 6 m depth.
source: BEU syllabus — Geotechnical Engineering-II, Unit 4

stem: Wash boring advances the hole by:
options: Chopping and jetting water that carries cuttings to the surface
explanation: Soil identification from the wash water is unreliable.
source: BEU syllabus — Geotechnical Engineering-II, Unit 4

stem: A major limitation of wash boring is that:
options: The washed cuttings give poor identification of the strata
explanation: Undisturbed samples must be taken at intervals.
source: BEU syllabus — Geotechnical Engineering-II, Unit 4

stem: Percussion drilling advances a borehole by:
options: Repeatedly raising and dropping a heavy chisel or bit
explanation: It suits boulders and hard strata but disturbs the soil below.
source: BEU syllabus — Geotechnical Engineering-II, Unit 4

stem: Rotary drilling is preferred for deep boreholes because it:
options: Is fast and can obtain good samples and rock cores
explanation: Drilling fluid stabilises the hole and removes cuttings.
source: BEU syllabus — Geotechnical Engineering-II, Unit 4

stem: A power auger with hollow stem is advantageous because it:
options: Allows sampling through the stem without withdrawing the auger
explanation: The hollow stem acts as temporary casing.
source: BEU syllabus — Geotechnical Engineering-II, Unit 4

stem: Boring in loose sand below the water table generally requires:
options: Casing or drilling mud to prevent collapse of the hole
explanation: Bentonite slurry supports the borehole wall.
source: BEU syllabus — Geotechnical Engineering-II, Unit 4

stem: Boring should not be advanced by bailing below the water table in sand because:
options: It causes piping and loosening of the soil beneath the hole
explanation: A positive water head must be maintained in the casing.
source: BEU syllabus — Geotechnical Engineering-II, Unit 4

stem: Sonic drilling advances the hole using:
options: High frequency vibration of the drill string
explanation: It gives high continuous core recovery in difficult ground.
source: BEU syllabus — Geotechnical Engineering-II, Unit 4

topic: Drilling in rock and borehole support
stem: Core drilling in rock uses:
options: A hollow core barrel with a diamond or tungsten carbide bit
explanation: The recovered core is logged and tested.
source: BEU syllabus — Geotechnical Engineering-II, Unit 4

topic: Drilling in rock and borehole support
stem: A double tube core barrel is preferred over a single tube because it:
options: Protects the core from the circulating fluid and improves recovery
explanation: Triple tube barrels give still better recovery in weak rock.
source: BEU syllabus — Geotechnical Engineering-II, Unit 4

topic: Drilling in rock and borehole support
stem: Drilling mud in a borehole serves to:
options: Stabilise the walls, cool the bit and carry cuttings to the surface
explanation: Bentonite forms a filter cake on the borehole wall.
source: BEU syllabus — Geotechnical Engineering-II, Unit 4

topic: Drilling in rock and borehole support
stem: Casing in a borehole is used to:
options: Prevent collapse of the sides and seal off unstable strata
explanation: It may be driven or installed as the hole advances.
source: BEU syllabus — Geotechnical Engineering-II, Unit 4

topic: Drilling in rock and borehole support
stem: A low RQD value in rock coring indicates:
options: Highly fractured or weathered rock of poor quality
explanation: RQD below 25 percent is classified as very poor.
source: BEU syllabus — Geotechnical Engineering-II, Unit 4

topic: Drilling in rock and borehole support
stem: Water loss during rock drilling indicates:
options: Open joints, cavities or fractures in the rock mass
explanation: Permeability or Lugeon tests quantify this.
source: BEU syllabus — Geotechnical Engineering-II, Unit 4

topic: Drilling in rock and borehole support
stem: A Lugeon test measures:
options: The water take of a packered borehole section under pressure
explanation: It is used in dam foundation grouting design.
source: BEU syllabus — Geotechnical Engineering-II, Unit 4

topic: Drilling in rock and borehole support
stem: Borehole cameras and televiewers are used to:
options: Record the orientation and condition of discontinuities in the borehole wall
explanation: They complement core logging when recovery is poor.
source: BEU syllabus — Geotechnical Engineering-II, Unit 4

topic: Drilling in rock and borehole support
stem: Grouting of a rock foundation is designed based on:
options: Water take results and joint patterns from the investigation
explanation: A curtain grout reduces seepage under dams.
source: BEU syllabus — Geotechnical Engineering-II, Unit 4

stem: A piezometer installed in a borehole measures:
options: Pore water pressure at a specific depth
explanation: A standpipe or vibrating wire piezometer may be used.
source: BEU syllabus — Geotechnical Engineering-II, Unit 4

stem: An open standpipe piezometer is unsuitable in low permeability clay because:
options: The response time is very long
explanation: Vibrating wire piezometers respond much faster.
source: BEU syllabus — Geotechnical Engineering-II, Unit 4

stem: Groundwater level must be recorded during boring because it:
options: Affects effective stress, bearing capacity and construction dewatering
explanation: Seasonal fluctuation should also be assessed.
source: BEU syllabus — Geotechnical Engineering-II, Unit 4

stem: An artesian condition encountered in a borehole means:
options: The piezometric level rises above the ground surface
explanation: Special care is required to prevent uncontrolled flow.
source: BEU syllabus — Geotechnical Engineering-II, Unit 4

stem: A borelog should record:
options: Depth, soil description, sample type and depth, SPT values and water level
explanation: Standardised soil description improves consistency.
source: BEU syllabus — Geotechnical Engineering-II, Unit 4

stem: A soil profile drawn from several borelogs is used to:
options: Interpolate the stratigraphy across the site for design
explanation: Interpolation between widely spaced holes carries uncertainty.
source: BEU syllabus — Geotechnical Engineering-II, Unit 4

stem: Boreholes must be backfilled or grouted after investigation to:
options: Prevent them becoming conduits for contamination between aquifers
explanation: It is a statutory good practice requirement.
source: BEU syllabus — Geotechnical Engineering-II, Unit 4

stem: An inclinometer casing installed in a borehole is used to monitor:
explanation: It is widely used for landslide and excavation monitoring.
source: BEU syllabus — Geotechnical Engineering-II, Unit 4

stem: A falling head permeability test in a borehole gives:
options: The in situ permeability of the surrounding stratum
explanation: Shape factors are applied to the borehole geometry.
source: BEU syllabus — Geotechnical Engineering-II, Unit 4

stem: A settlement marker or magnetic extensometer is installed to:
options: Measure the compression of individual soil layers with depth
explanation: It verifies design settlement predictions during construction.
source: BEU syllabus — Geotechnical Engineering-II, Unit 4

stem: Wash boring gives reliable identification of the strata penetrated.
explanation: The washed cuttings are mixed and give only crude identification.
source: BEU syllabus — Geotechnical Engineering-II, Unit 4

topic: Drilling in rock and borehole support
stem: A double tube core barrel improves core recovery in weak rock.
explanation: The inner tube shields the core from the circulating drilling fluid.
source: BEU syllabus — Geotechnical Engineering-II, Unit 4

stem:
Assertion (A): A positive water head must be maintained in the casing when boring in sand below the water table.
Reason (R): A lower head inside allows upward seepage that loosens and heaves the soil at the base of the hole.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: This would render subsequent SPT results meaningless.
source: BEU syllabus — Geotechnical Engineering-II, Unit 4

stem:
Assertion (A): Vibrating wire piezometers are preferred in clays.
Reason (R): Their very small water volume requirement gives a rapid response in low permeability soils.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Open standpipes may take weeks to equilibrate in clay.
source: BEU syllabus — Geotechnical Engineering-II, Unit 4

stem: Which are recognised methods of advancing a borehole?
explanation: Consolidation testing is a laboratory test, not a boring method.
source: BEU syllabus — Geotechnical Engineering-II, Unit 4

stem: Ultimate bearing capacity of a soil is:
options: The maximum pressure the soil can support without shear failure
explanation: Safe bearing capacity applies a factor of safety.
source: BEU syllabus — Geotechnical Engineering-II, Unit 5

stem: Allowable bearing pressure is governed by:
options: The lower of the shear failure and settlement criteria
explanation: In sands settlement usually governs.
source: BEU syllabus — Geotechnical Engineering-II, Unit 5

stem: Terzaghi's bearing capacity equation for a strip footing is:
explanation: Shape factors modify it for square and circular footings.
source: BEU syllabus — Geotechnical Engineering-II, Unit 5

stem: For a saturated clay under undrained conditions, Nc is taken as:
explanation: Nq equals 1 and N gamma equals 0 for phi equal to zero.
source: BEU syllabus — Geotechnical Engineering-II, Unit 5

stem: Local shear failure occurs in:
options: Loose sands and soft clays with large settlement before failure
explanation: Strength parameters are reduced by two thirds in the analysis.
source: BEU syllabus — Geotechnical Engineering-II, Unit 5

stem: Raising the water table to the base of a footing in sand:
options: Reduces the bearing capacity roughly by half
explanation: The submerged unit weight is about half the bulk value.
source: BEU syllabus — Geotechnical Engineering-II, Unit 5

stem: A raft foundation is preferred when:
options: Individual footings would cover more than about half the plan area
explanation: It also reduces differential settlement.
source: BEU syllabus — Geotechnical Engineering-II, Unit 5

stem: A floating or compensated raft works on the principle that:
options: The weight of excavated soil offsets the structural load
explanation: Net increase in stress is minimised.
source: BEU syllabus — Geotechnical Engineering-II, Unit 5

stem: Eccentric loading on a footing is treated by:
options: Using an effective reduced footing area concentric with the load
explanation: Meyerhof's effective width approach is standard.
source: BEU syllabus — Geotechnical Engineering-II, Unit 5

stem: Piles are used when:
options: Shallow strata are weak and loads must be transferred to deeper firm strata
The soil is strong at the surface
explanation: They also resist uplift and lateral loads.
source: BEU syllabus — Geotechnical Engineering-II, Unit 5

stem: The ultimate load capacity of a pile is the sum of:
options: End bearing resistance and skin friction resistance

source: BEU syllabus — Geotechnical Engineering-II, Unit 5

stem: A friction pile carries load mainly by:
options: Skin friction along the pile shaft
explanation: An end bearing pile rests on a firm stratum.
source: BEU syllabus — Geotechnical Engineering-II, Unit 5

stem: The alpha method estimates pile skin friction in clay from:
options: An adhesion factor times the undrained shear strength
explanation: Alpha decreases as the clay strength increases.
source: BEU syllabus — Geotechnical Engineering-II, Unit 5

stem: Negative skin friction on a pile occurs when:
options: Surrounding soil settles more than the pile, dragging it down
explanation: It adds load rather than resistance to the pile.
source: BEU syllabus — Geotechnical Engineering-II, Unit 5

stem: The efficiency of a pile group in clay is generally:
options: Less than unity due to overlapping stress zones
explanation: Block failure of the group must also be checked.
source: BEU syllabus — Geotechnical Engineering-II, Unit 5

stem: A pile load test is conducted to:
options: Verify the load capacity and load settlement behaviour in the field
explanation: Initial and routine tests are specified in IS 2911.
source: BEU syllabus — Geotechnical Engineering-II, Unit 5

stem: A well or caisson foundation is commonly used for:
options: Bridge piers in rivers where scour depth is large
explanation: It must be taken below the maximum scour depth with adequate grip length.
source: BEU syllabus — Geotechnical Engineering-II, Unit 5

stem: Under reamed piles are particularly suited to:
options: Expansive black cotton soils to resist uplift from swelling
explanation: The bulb anchors the pile below the active zone.
source: BEU syllabus — Geotechnical Engineering-II, Unit 5

stem: Pile integrity testing by low strain method detects:
options: Defects such as necking or discontinuity in the shaft
explanation: It is a rapid non destructive quality control method.
source: BEU syllabus — Geotechnical Engineering-II, Unit 5

topic: Earth pressure, retaining structures and ground improvement
stem: Active earth pressure develops when a retaining wall:
explanation: Passive pressure develops when the wall moves into the soil.
source: BEU syllabus — Geotechnical Engineering-II, Unit 5

topic: Earth pressure, retaining structures and ground improvement
stem: The coefficient of active earth pressure for a smooth vertical wall with horizontal cohesionless backfill is:

topic: Earth pressure, retaining structures and ground improvement
stem: At rest earth pressure coefficient for a normally consolidated soil is approximately:
explanation: This is Jaky's formula.
source: BEU syllabus — Geotechnical Engineering-II, Unit 5

topic: Earth pressure, retaining structures and ground improvement
stem: Rankine's theory of earth pressure assumes:
options: A smooth vertical wall with no friction between wall and soil

source: BEU syllabus — Geotechnical Engineering-II, Unit 5

topic: Earth pressure, retaining structures and ground improvement
stem: Retaining wall stability checks include:

source: BEU syllabus — Geotechnical Engineering-II, Unit 5

topic: Earth pressure, retaining structures and ground improvement
stem: A weep hole in a retaining wall is provided to:

source: BEU syllabus — Geotechnical Engineering-II, Unit 5

topic: Earth pressure, retaining structures and ground improvement
stem: Sheet pile walls in deep excavations are supported by:

source: BEU syllabus — Geotechnical Engineering-II, Unit 5

topic: Earth pressure, retaining structures and ground improvement
stem: Dynamic compaction improves ground by:

explanation: It is effective in loose granular fills.
source: BEU syllabus — Geotechnical Engineering-II, Unit 5

topic: Earth pressure, retaining structures and ground improvement
stem: Stone columns improve soft clay by:

stem: Negative skin friction adds to the load on a pile rather than to its capacity.

source: BEU syllabus — Geotechnical Engineering-II, Unit 5

topic: Earth pressure, retaining structures and ground improvement
stem: Passive earth pressure is smaller than active earth pressure.

source: BEU syllabus — Geotechnical Engineering-II, Unit 5

stem:
Assertion (A): Bearing capacity of a footing in sand nearly halves when the water table rises to the base level.

Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A

A is false but R is true

stem: Which stability checks are required for a gravity retaining wall?

explanation: Monitoring and feedback are central to it.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective: Environmental Systems [101611], Unit 4

topic: Uncertainty, risk and robustness in tradeoff analysis
stem: Deep uncertainty differs from ordinary uncertainty because:
options: Parties cannot agree on the models or the probability distributions themselves
explanation: Robust decision making methods are used.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective: Environmental Systems [101611], Unit 4

topic: Multi objective optimisation and Pareto tradeoffs
stem: Presenting the Pareto front to decision makers is useful because it:
options: Separates technical analysis from the value judgement of choosing a point
explanation: This is the generate first, choose later philosophy.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective: Environmental Systems [101611], Unit 4

topic: Multi objective optimisation and Pareto tradeoffs
stem: A dominated solution can never be part of the Pareto front.
explanation: By definition another solution is at least as good in all objectives and better in one.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective: Environmental Systems [101611], Unit 4

topic: Methods for generating and selecting among tradeoffs
stem: The weighting method can generate all points of a non convex Pareto front.
explanation: Weighted sums cannot reach non convex portions; the constraint method can.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective: Environmental Systems [101611], Unit 4

topic: Methods for generating and selecting among tradeoffs
stem:
Assertion (A): Analysts should generate the tradeoff set before a final choice is made.
Reason (R): Choosing among Pareto optimal options involves value judgements that belong to decision makers and stakeholders.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: This separates analysis from preference.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective: Environmental Systems [101611], Unit 4

topic: Uncertainty, risk and robustness in tradeoff analysis
stem:
Assertion (A): Robust solutions may be preferred over optimal ones in environmental planning.
Reason (R): Deep uncertainty about future conditions means an optimum for one scenario can fail badly in others.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Performance across scenarios is evaluated.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective: Environmental Systems [101611], Unit 4

topic: Methods for generating and selecting among tradeoffs
stem: Which are multi objective analysis techniques?
explanation: A mass balance is a modelling relationship, not a multi objective technique.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective: Environmental Systems [101611], Unit 4

topic: Case study: river water quality management
stem: The Streeter Phelps equation describes:
options: The dissolved oxygen sag in a river downstream of a waste discharge
explanation: Deoxygenation and reaeration are balanced.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective: Environmental Systems [101611], Unit 5

topic: Case study: river water quality management
stem: The critical point in a dissolved oxygen sag curve is where:
options: The dissolved oxygen concentration is minimum
explanation: It determines whether standards are violated.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective: Environmental Systems [101611], Unit 5

topic: Case study: river water quality management
stem: The deoxygenation rate constant in the Streeter Phelps model represents:
options: The rate of oxygen consumption by biochemical oxidation of organic matter
explanation: It increases with temperature.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective: Environmental Systems [101611], Unit 5

topic: Case study: river water quality management
stem: Reaeration in a river increases with:
options: Higher velocity, turbulence and lower depth
explanation: O'Connor Dobbins type formulas relate it to velocity and depth.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective: Environmental Systems [101611], Unit 5

topic: Case study: river water quality management
stem: Total maximum daily load for a water body is:
options: The maximum pollutant load it can receive and still meet standards
explanation: It is allocated among point and non point sources.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective: Environmental Systems [101611], Unit 5

topic: Case study: river water quality management
stem: Least cost waste load allocation using LP determines:
options: Treatment levels at each discharger that meet quality standards at minimum total cost
explanation: Uniform treatment is usually more costly overall.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective: Environmental Systems [101611], Unit 5

topic: Case study: river water quality management
stem: Equity concerns in waste load allocation arise because:
options: Least cost solutions may require very different treatment levels from different dischargers
explanation: Equity based formulations are sometimes used instead.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective: Environmental Systems [101611], Unit 5

topic: Case study: river water quality management
stem: Low flow conditions such as the 7Q10 flow are used in water quality planning because:
options: They represent the critical condition with least dilution
explanation: 7Q10 is the seven day low flow with a ten year return period.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective: Environmental Systems [101611], Unit 5

topic: Case study: river water quality management
stem: Non point source pollution is harder to manage than point sources because it:
options: Is diffuse, weather driven and difficult to measure and regulate
explanation: Best management practices are used instead of permits.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective: Environmental Systems [101611], Unit 5

topic: Case study: water supply and reservoir systems
stem: A reservoir operation policy specifies:
options: Releases as a function of storage, inflow and time of year
explanation: Rule curves express the policy graphically.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective: Environmental Systems [101611], Unit 5

topic: Case study: water supply and reservoir systems
stem: A rule curve for a multipurpose reservoir defines:
options: Target storage levels through the year balancing conservation and flood control
explanation: Flood cushion is kept before the monsoon.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective: Environmental Systems [101611], Unit 5

topic: Case study: water supply and reservoir systems
stem: Reservoir yield analysis determines:
options: The dependable supply that can be drawn for a given reliability
explanation: Sequent peak analysis is one method.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective: Environmental Systems [101611], Unit 5

topic: Case study: water supply and reservoir systems
stem: Conjunctive use of surface water and groundwater aims to:
options: Use both sources in a coordinated way to increase reliability and reduce cost
explanation: Aquifers can store surplus surface water.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective: Environmental Systems [101611], Unit 5

topic: Case study: water supply and reservoir systems
stem: Optimisation of a water distribution network typically minimises:
options: Capital and pumping cost subject to demand and pressure constraints
explanation: The problem is nonlinear and often solved by heuristics.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective: Environmental Systems [101611], Unit 5

topic: Case study: water supply and reservoir systems
stem: Demand management in water supply includes:
options: Leakage reduction, metering, tariffs and efficient fixtures
explanation: It is often cheaper than augmenting supply.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective: Environmental Systems [101611], Unit 5

topic: Case study: water supply and reservoir systems
stem: Reliability of a water supply system is measured as:
options: The proportion of time or volume for which demand is fully met
explanation: Resilience and vulnerability complement it.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective: Environmental Systems [101611], Unit 5

topic: Case study: water supply and reservoir systems
stem: Stochastic dynamic programming is used in reservoir operation to:
options: Optimise releases when inflows are random
explanation: Transition probabilities of inflow states are used.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective: Environmental Systems [101611], Unit 5

topic: Case study: water supply and reservoir systems
stem: Environmental or ecological flow requirements in reservoir operation:
options: Reserve a minimum release to sustain downstream ecosystems
explanation: They compete with consumptive uses.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective: Environmental Systems [101611], Unit 5

stem: A Gaussian plume model predicts:
options: Downwind ground level concentrations from a continuous point source
explanation: It assumes normal distributions of concentration crosswind and vertically.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective: Environmental Systems [101611], Unit 5

stem: Effective stack height in plume modelling is:
options: The physical stack height plus the plume rise
explanation: Buoyancy and momentum cause the rise.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective: Environmental Systems [101611], Unit 5

stem: Atmospheric stability class affects dispersion because:
options: Unstable conditions promote mixing while stable conditions suppress it
explanation: Pasquill stability classes are used.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective: Environmental Systems [101611], Unit 5

stem: Ground level concentration downwind of a stack generally:
options: Rises to a maximum at some distance and then decreases
explanation: Taller stacks move the maximum farther and lower it.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective: Environmental Systems [101611], Unit 5

stem: An emission inventory for air quality management lists:
options: Sources and their quantified emissions of each pollutant
explanation: It is the basis for source apportionment and control planning.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective: Environmental Systems [101611], Unit 5

stem: Receptor modelling in air quality is used to:
options: Apportion measured ambient concentrations among likely source categories
explanation: Chemical mass balance and factor analysis are used.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective: Environmental Systems [101611], Unit 5

stem: An air quality index is used to:
options: Communicate air quality to the public on a simple scale
explanation: It aggregates several pollutants into one number.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective: Environmental Systems [101611], Unit 5

stem: Least cost air pollution control planning uses optimisation to:
options: Select control measures at sources to meet ambient standards at minimum cost
explanation: Transfer coefficients link emissions to receptor concentrations.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective: Environmental Systems [101611], Unit 5

stem: Tall stacks reduce local ground level concentrations but:
options: Transport pollutants farther and can worsen regional problems
explanation: Dilution is not a substitute for emission reduction.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective: Environmental Systems [101611], Unit 5

topic: Case study: river water quality management
stem: The critical deficit point in the oxygen sag curve gives the minimum dissolved oxygen.
explanation: It is the governing condition for water quality standards downstream of a discharge.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective: Environmental Systems [101611], Unit 5

stem: Increasing stack height reduces the total mass of pollutant emitted.
explanation: It only disperses the same emissions more widely; total emission is unchanged.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective: Environmental Systems [101611], Unit 5

topic: Case study: river water quality management
stem:
Assertion (A): Low flow conditions are used for waste load allocation studies.
Reason (R): Minimum flow provides the least dilution and therefore the most critical water quality condition.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: The 7Q10 flow is a common design value.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective: Environmental Systems [101611], Unit 5

topic: Case study: water supply and reservoir systems
stem:
Assertion (A): Conjunctive use of surface water and groundwater increases system reliability.
Reason (R): Aquifer storage can buffer surface water shortfalls during droughts and store surpluses in wet years.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Coordinated operation is required.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective: Environmental Systems [101611], Unit 5

topic: Case study: river water quality management
stem: Which factors affect the dissolved oxygen profile of a river below a discharge?
options: Reaeration rate governed by velocity and depth
explanation: Bed colour has no bearing on the oxygen balance.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective: Environmental Systems [101611], Unit 5

topic: Case study: solid and hazardous waste systems
stem: The waste management hierarchy places at the highest priority:
explanation: Reuse and recycling follow prevention.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective: Environmental Systems [101611], Unit 6

topic: Case study: solid and hazardous waste systems
stem: Systems analysis of solid waste collection typically addresses:
options: Vehicle routing, transfer station siting and crew scheduling
explanation: Routing problems are combinatorial optimisation problems.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective: Environmental Systems [101611], Unit 6

topic: Case study: solid and hazardous waste systems
stem: A transfer station is economically justified when:
options: Haul distance to the disposal site is long relative to collection vehicle economics
explanation: Larger vehicles then carry the bulk haul.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective: Environmental Systems [101611], Unit 6

topic: Case study: solid and hazardous waste systems
stem: Landfill siting analysis uses GIS overlays to:
options: Screen candidate sites against hydrogeological, distance and land use criteria
explanation: Multi criteria evaluation ranks the shortlisted sites.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective: Environmental Systems [101611], Unit 6

topic: Case study: solid and hazardous waste systems
stem: Landfill gas from anaerobic decomposition consists mainly of:
explanation: Capture and energy recovery reduce emissions.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective: Environmental Systems [101611], Unit 6

topic: Case study: solid and hazardous waste systems
stem: Leachate management at a landfill requires:
options: Liner, collection system and treatment before discharge
explanation: Groundwater monitoring wells are also required.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective: Environmental Systems [101611], Unit 6

topic: Case study: solid and hazardous waste systems
stem: Source segregation of municipal solid waste improves the system because:
options: Recyclables stay clean and organic waste can be composted or digested
explanation: Mixed waste is much harder to process.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective: Environmental Systems [101611], Unit 6

topic: Case study: solid and hazardous waste systems
stem: Hazardous waste management requires cradle to grave tracking because:
options: Responsibility for safe handling extends from generation through final disposal
explanation: Manifest systems record each transfer.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective: Environmental Systems [101611], Unit 6

topic: Case study: solid and hazardous waste systems
stem: Waste to energy plants are evaluated in systems analysis considering:
options: Calorific value, capital cost, emissions and competition with recycling
explanation: Low calorific mixed waste performs poorly.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective: Environmental Systems [101611], Unit 6

topic: Case study: energy, climate and industrial ecology
stem: Industrial ecology views industrial systems as:
options: Analogous to ecosystems where wastes of one process become inputs to another
explanation: Eco industrial parks apply the concept.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective: Environmental Systems [101611], Unit 6

topic: Case study: energy, climate and industrial ecology
stem: Industrial symbiosis involves:
options: Exchange of materials, energy and water among neighbouring industries
explanation: Kalundborg in Denmark is the best known example.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective: Environmental Systems [101611], Unit 6

topic: Case study: energy, climate and industrial ecology
stem: Life cycle assessment stages defined by ISO 14040 are:
options: Goal and scope, inventory analysis, impact assessment and interpretation
explanation: The functional unit is defined in the scope.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective: Environmental Systems [101611], Unit 6

topic: Case study: energy, climate and industrial ecology
stem: The functional unit in an LCA is:
options: The quantified performance of the product system used as the reference
explanation: It makes alternatives comparable.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective: Environmental Systems [101611], Unit 6

topic: Case study: energy, climate and industrial ecology
stem: Carbon footprint of a product measures:
options: The greenhouse gas emissions associated with its life cycle
explanation: Results are expressed as carbon dioxide equivalent.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective: Environmental Systems [101611], Unit 6

topic: Case study: energy, climate and industrial ecology
stem: Energy systems optimisation for a region typically decides:
options: The mix and timing of generation and efficiency investments at least cost
explanation: Emission constraints can be added.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective: Environmental Systems [101611], Unit 6

topic: Case study: energy, climate and industrial ecology
stem: A marginal abatement cost curve for greenhouse gases ranks:
options: Mitigation measures by cost per tonne of carbon dioxide avoided
explanation: Negative cost measures are win win options.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective: Environmental Systems [101611], Unit 6

topic: Case study: energy, climate and industrial ecology
stem: Allocation problems in LCA arise when:
options: A process yields several products and impacts must be divided among them
explanation: System expansion is one way to avoid allocation.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective: Environmental Systems [101611], Unit 6

topic: Case study: energy, climate and industrial ecology
stem: Burden shifting in environmental analysis means:
options: Reducing one impact or life stage while increasing another
explanation: Full life cycle analysis reveals it.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective: Environmental Systems [101611], Unit 6

stem: Integrated water resources management is defined by:
options: Coordinated development of water, land and related resources for equitable welfare
explanation: River basin is the natural planning unit.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective: Environmental Systems [101611], Unit 6

stem: River basin scale planning is preferred because:
options: Hydrological processes and upstream downstream effects cross administrative boundaries
explanation: Basin organisations coordinate the stakeholders.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective: Environmental Systems [101611], Unit 6

stem: A key challenge in implementing systems analysis results is:
options: Institutional, political and stakeholder acceptance of the recommended solution
explanation: Technically optimal solutions may be politically infeasible.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective: Environmental Systems [101611], Unit 6

stem: Data availability limits environmental systems analysis because:
options: Model calibration and reliable conclusions require adequate monitoring data
explanation: Investment in monitoring networks is essential.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective: Environmental Systems [101611], Unit 6

stem: A decision support system for environmental management combines:
options: Models, databases and a user interface to aid decision makers
explanation: Scenario comparison is a typical feature.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective: Environmental Systems [101611], Unit 6

stem: Capacity building is needed alongside analytical tools because:
options: Local staff must be able to operate, interpret and update the models
explanation: Otherwise tools fall into disuse after the project.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective: Environmental Systems [101611], Unit 6

stem: Monitoring and evaluation of an implemented environmental plan provides:
options: Feedback to verify performance and revise the plan
explanation: It supports adaptive management.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective: Environmental Systems [101611], Unit 6

stem: A common reason environmental optimisation results are not implemented is:
options: Equity, legal or institutional constraints not represented in the model
explanation: Post optimality discussion with stakeholders is important.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective: Environmental Systems [101611], Unit 6

stem: Sustainability indicators for a city are used to:
options: Track progress on environmental, social and economic performance over time
explanation: Baselines and targets make them meaningful.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective: Environmental Systems [101611], Unit 6

topic: Case study: solid and hazardous waste systems
stem: The waste management hierarchy places landfilling above prevention.
explanation: Prevention is the highest priority and landfilling the lowest.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective: Environmental Systems [101611], Unit 6

topic: Case study: energy, climate and industrial ecology
stem: Life cycle assessment considers impacts from raw material extraction to disposal.
explanation: This cradle to grave scope is what distinguishes LCA from single stage analysis.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective: Environmental Systems [101611], Unit 6

stem:
Assertion (A): Technically optimal environmental solutions are sometimes not implemented.
Reason (R): Institutional, equity and political constraints not captured in the model can make them unacceptable.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Stakeholder engagement helps identify these constraints.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective: Environmental Systems [101611], Unit 6

topic: Case study: energy, climate and industrial ecology
stem:
Assertion (A): Full life cycle analysis is needed to avoid burden shifting.
Reason (R): A measure that reduces impact at one stage may increase it at another stage or in another impact category.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Only a complete accounting reveals the net effect.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective: Environmental Systems [101611], Unit 6

topic: Case study: energy, climate and industrial ecology
stem: Which are stages of a life cycle assessment as defined by ISO 14040?
explanation: Tender evaluation is a procurement activity.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective: Environmental Systems [101611], Unit 6

subject_name: Program Elective: Design of Hydraulic Structures/Irrigation Engineering [101612]
stem: A canal that takes its supply directly from a river is called a:
explanation: It feeds branch canals and distributaries.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective: Design of Hydraulic Structures/Irrigation Engineering [101612], Unit 1

subject_name: Program Elective: Design of Hydraulic Structures/Irrigation Engineering [101612]
stem: An inundation canal:
options: Draws water only during the high flood stage of a river
explanation: A perennial canal is fed from a weir or barrage.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective: Design of Hydraulic Structures/Irrigation Engineering [101612], Unit 1

subject_name: Program Elective: Design of Hydraulic Structures/Irrigation Engineering [101612]
stem: A ridge or watershed canal is advantageous because:
options: It can irrigate on both sides and needs no cross drainage works
explanation: Contour canals irrigate only on one side.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective: Design of Hydraulic Structures/Irrigation Engineering [101612], Unit 1

subject_name: Program Elective: Design of Hydraulic Structures/Irrigation Engineering [101612]
stem: A contour canal:
options: Follows a contour with a slight slope and irrigates on one side only
explanation: It requires cross drainage works for streams it crosses.
source: BEU syllabus — Program Elective: Design of Hydraulic Structures/Irrigation Engineering [101612], Unit 1

subject_name: Program Elective: Design of Hydraulic Structures/Irrigation Engineering [101612]
stem: Gross command area is:
options: The total area that can be commanded by a canal irrespective of culturability
explanation: Culturable command area excludes barren and built up land.
